name: Field Horsetail Tea
use: Headache relief
method: Field horsetail was chewed or brewed into a tea to ease head pain.
note: Horsetail's rough, gritty texture — it was once used to scour pots and polish wood — may be exactly why chewing or brewing it felt like it was doing something concrete for a headache. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy's Great Law of Peace, a system of checks, balances, and consensus government among six nations, is widely credited by historians as an influence on Benjamin Franklin and the framers of the U.S. Constitution.

name: Spruce Needle Tea
use: Preventing and treating scurvy
method: Fresh spruce needles, rich in vitamin C, were steeped into a strong tea.
note: The needles' sharp, resinous taste was impossible to mistake for anything else, which mattered when a whole family's winter health depended on gathering the right plant. Haudenosaunee wampum belts weren't just beadwork, either — woven shell-bead patterns served as an actual written record of treaties, laws, and history.

name: Witch Hazel Wash
use: Bruises, insect bites, minor skin irritation
method: Bark and leaves were boiled down into a soothing wash applied to the skin, or preserved in alcohol as a tincture for a stronger, longer-lasting version — closer to the distilled witch hazel extract still sold in drugstores today.
note: The name has nothing to do with witchcraft — “wicke” is Old English for bendable or pliant, describing the plant's flexible branches. Colonists simply carried that English word over to a plant they'd learned about from Northeastern nations.

name: Cranberry
use: General wellness and wound treatment
method: Berries were harvested from Northeastern bogs — often by flooding the bog and skimming the berries as they floated free — then eaten fresh, dried for winter, or mashed into poultices for wounds.
note: That same flood-harvest trick is still how cranberries are commercially harvested today. The Wampanoag are a living nation, not a “first Thanksgiving” relic — the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project has spent decades rebuilding their language from 17th-century written records, after it had no living fluent speakers left by the early 1900s.

name: Boneset Tea
people: Native peoples of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Fevers and flu-like illness (“breakbone fever”)
method: Dried leaves and flowering tops were steeped into a famously bitter tea, drunk scalding hot while the patient was bundled under heavy blankets to bring on a sweat. Nineteenth-century physicians who wanted a milder, more measurable dose also preserved it as a fluid extract or tincture.
note: European colonists — English, German, and others — widely adopted boneset for feverish illness by the 1700s, and bundles of it once hung from cabin rafters across early America.
caution: Brewed too strong or drunk cold, it was known to trigger vomiting instead — see “Setting the Record Straight” below for what modern medicine says about sweating out a fever.

name: Sumac Berry Syrup
use: Diarrhea and digestive upset
method: Tart berries, picked just before the first frost, were cooked into a thick astringent syrup.
note: Picking at exactly that moment — just before frost sharpened their sourness — was a matter of careful seasonal timing passed down through generations, not guesswork. That same tradition of exact, systematic plant knowledge later helped Cherokee scholar Sequoyah invent a complete writing system from scratch in the 1820s.

name: Dried Fruit Bread
use: Digestive upset
method: Wild fruit was sun-dried to concentrate its natural astringency, then baked into a bread — a form gentle enough for an unsettled stomach to actually keep down.
note: That kind of practical thinking, turning a harsh remedy into something the body could tolerate, came from the same nation who, just sixteen years after their own forced removal on the Trail of Tears, raised and sent famine relief to Ireland in 1847. A sculpture called Kindred Spirits stands in County Cork today, honoring that gift.

name: Wart Poultice
use: Removing warts
method: A poultice made from wild fruit was applied directly to the skin and renewed day after day until the wart was gone.
note: That kind of patient repetition — a poultice reapplied daily rather than one strong dose — reflects how much old medicine relied on watching results over time. The Catawba are one of the few Southeastern nations who never left their ancestral homeland in South Carolina, despite the U.S. government terminating their federal recognition in 1959 and not restoring it until 1993.

name: Root Bark Worm Tea
use: Expelling intestinal parasites
method: A strong tea was brewed from root bark and drunk over several consecutive days rather than all at once.
note: Drinking it gradually matched how the Muscogee understood parasites — a problem driven out over time, not solved in a single dose. The same nation held an annual Green Corn Ceremony that worked almost like a yearly reset, forgiving grudges and relighting the town's ceremonial fire to start the year clean.

name: Bark Chew for Heartburn
use: Heartburn relief
method: A piece of bark was simply chewed slowly to calm the stomach — no fire and no water needed.
note: That portability made it one of the simplest remedies in this whole archive: just the tree itself, wherever you happened to be. The Rappahannock who relied on it didn't regain federal recognition until 2018, one of the most recent tribes to receive it, after Virginia's early-20th-century “Racial Integrity Act” spent decades trying to erase Native identity from official records.

name: Echinacea Root
use: Wounds, sore throats, infections, and bites
method: The root was chewed raw or brewed into a strong tea, or preserved as a tincture — chopped root packed in a jar, covered with strong spirits, and left to steep for several weeks before straining.
note: Chewing the raw root produced an unmistakable tingling, numbing sensation on the tongue — a sensory clue Plains peoples took seriously as a sign of real medicinal strength, and one reason echinacea went on to become one of the best-selling herbal supplements in the United States. The Lakota and other Plains nations also kept “winter counts,” pictographic calendars on hide recording one major event per year, some running unbroken for over a century.

name: Berry Tea Gargle
use: Sore, inflamed throats
method: A tea brewed from wild berries was gargled rather than swallowed, keeping the most astringent part of the remedy working right where the throat was sore.
note: For over a century, the Comanche were the dominant power across a vast stretch of the Southern Plains called Comancheria, effectively limiting Spanish, Mexican, and early American expansion into Texas — and Comanche code talkers later served in World War II alongside their better-known Navajo counterparts.

name: Root Eyewash
use: Eye irritation
method: Plant roots were simmered down into a gentle decoction, deliberately diluted for something as sensitive as the eyes, and used to rinse them.
note: The Potawatomi were part of the long-standing Council of Three Fires, a political and military alliance with the Ojibwe and Odawa nations that coordinated diplomacy and defense across the Great Lakes for generations.

name: Spreading Dogbane
use: Headache relief
method: The plant was prepared and taken specifically to relieve head pain, a use refined the way most old medicine was — tried, remembered, and kept only when it actually seemed to help, generation after generation.
note: Ojibwe Midewiwin societies recorded ceremonies and history on birchbark scrolls called wiigwaasabak, symbols pressed into the bark — a genuine pre-contact recording system, not simply the oral-only tradition it's often flattened into.

name: Juniper Tea
use: Colds, flu, headaches, and stomachaches
method: Juniper needles and berries were steeped into an all-purpose tea.
note: Juniper's sharp, resinous smell was part of why it became a true cure-all across the desert Southwest — abundant and strong-smelling enough that reaching for it for almost anything made practical sense. The Hopi village of Old Oraibi has been continuously inhabited since roughly 1100 CE, sustained by dry-farming techniques that grow corn in the desert without irrigation.

name: Coyote Tobacco Smoke
use: Headache relief
method: Wild coyote tobacco was smoked in small amounts.
note: Distinct from cultivated tobacco, this wild variety held a specific medicinal role rather than everyday use. Diné healing traditions center on Hózhó — living in balance and beauty — so a remedy like this was never just about the symptom, but one piece of restoring a person's whole state of harmony. Navajo Marines later carried their language into World War II as an unbroken code no enemy cryptographer ever solved.

name: California Poppy Rinse
use: Treating head lice
method: California poppy flowers were steeped into a strong tea and used as a rinse.
note: That same poppy is now California's official state flower — a plant that once did practical double duty as lice medicine for Costanoan families. In the 1850s the U.S. Senate secretly negotiated eighteen treaties with California tribes, then rejected all of them and sealed the records for over fifty years.

name: Seed & Bear-Fat Hair Tonic
use: Hair and scalp care
method: Crushed seeds were mixed with bear fat and worked into the hair.
note: Mixing the seeds into fat rather than water gave the tonic real staying power — a fat-based base held plant compounds against the scalp far longer than any rinse could. Ohlone people were declared administratively extinct in some 20th-century records despite never disappearing; descendant communities like the Muwekma Ohlone are actively rebuilding language and culture today.

name: Household Herb Gardens
use: The family's everyday medicine chest
method: Women tended kitchen gardens of imported and local herbs, often laid out as a deliberate “physic garden” divided into quadrants, then distilled and prepared remedies for the household.
note: That layout was a direct copy of English apothecary garden traditions carried across the Atlantic. Most 17th-century English arrivals to the colonies weren't free settlers chasing religious freedom, either — the majority came as indentured servants, bound to years of unpaid labor just to pay for their passage.

name: Sassafras Root Tonic
people: English & other European colonists (a practice learned from Native peoples)
use: Spring “blood purifier” tonic
method: Root bark was boiled into a tea taken as a seasonal cleanse, or preserved as a bitters-style tincture in spirits.
note: Sassafras was briefly one of colonial Virginia's most valuable export crops, so prized in Europe that early shipments rivaled tobacco in value — a boom that collapsed almost as fast as it began.
caution: Sassafras contains safrole, now recognized as a liver toxin. It's listed here for historical interest only.

name: Catnip Colic Tea
use: Soothing infant colic
method: A mild catnip tea was given to fussy babies in small doses.
note: Catnip's gentle, almost sweet smell made it one of the few strong-tasting remedies a fussy baby wouldn't immediately fight. “Pennsylvania Dutch” is actually a mistranslation — “Dutch” comes from “Deitsch,” their word for German — and the dialect is still spoken today among Old Order Amish and Mennonite communities.

name: Sage Cold Tea
use: Common colds
method: Garden sage was brewed into a warming tea at the first sign of a cold.
note: Sage's peppery bite was exactly why it got reached for so quickly — a plant whose effect you could feel immediately mattered when you had no other way to know whether a remedy was working. Pennsylvania German healers blended this kind of herbalism with prayer in a tradition called Braucherei, whose most famous printed source became a folk-medicine bestseller still reprinted today.

name: Yarrow
use: Bleeding, inflammation, and fever
method: Fresh leaves were pressed directly onto small wounds, dried flowers were powdered and packed into deeper cuts to help stop bleeding, the leaves were brewed as tea for fever, and it was sometimes preserved as a tincture in spirits for a stronger, longer-lasting version.
note: Called “soldier's woundwort” for its battlefield reputation, and one of the most widely used herbs in colonial Pennsylvania.
caution: Traditionally avoided internally during pregnancy, since it was understood as a uterine stimulant.

name: Wormwood Bitters
use: General tonic and digestive complaints
method: Wormwood was infused in spirits or water as a bitter tonic — essentially a home tincture, taken in small doses before or after meals.
note: Wormwood's intense bitterness was the whole point — old medicine often equated a strong, unpleasant taste with real potency. Pennsylvania German communities were also known for fraktur, elaborately hand-illustrated birth and baptismal certificates, showing the same careful attention to record-keeping.

name: Nopal (Prickly Pear) Poultice
use: Wounds and inflammation
method: The pad of the prickly pear cactus was split open and applied directly to the skin — no drying or brewing needed.
note: That immediacy is part of why it's still a living practice in Mexican-American folk medicine today. Spanish Florida's St. Augustine, founded in 1565, predates Jamestown and Plymouth by decades; the mission system that helped spread this plant knowledge also relied heavily on forced Indigenous labor — a history worth naming alongside what it preserved.

name: Root Doctors & Granny Women
use: Healing across many everyday ailments
method: Respected healers known as “root doctors” and “granny women” foraged forest and wetland plants, then prepared them as teas, poultices, and washes fitted to whatever a family could gather nearby.
note: Enslavers specifically sought captives from West Africa's “Rice Coast” for their existing rice-farming expertise — a fact that quietly undercuts the old myth of enslaved people as unskilled labor. That same depth of transported knowledge extended directly into medicine.

name: Foraged Forest & Wetland Remedies
people: African American communities across the South
use: Wound care, fevers, and everyday illness
method: Plants were gathered from forests and wetlands near plantations rather than grown openly, then prepared as whatever the specific plant called for — tea, poultice, or wash.
note: Root doctors drew on specific West and Central African plant knowledge — some tracing to Kongo spiritual-medical traditions — blended with what enslaved communities learned from Native neighbors. Well into the 20th century, granny midwives carrying this same tradition still delivered most babies born across large parts of the rural South.

name: Yellowroot
use: Tonic, digestive complaints, mouth sores, jaundice
method: The bright yellow root was chewed fresh, simmered into a bitter decoction, or preserved as a tincture in spirits for a remedy that lasted the whole season.
note: The root's intense bitterness and bright yellow color were themselves the clue old healers went on — a taste and color unmistakable enough to be remembered and passed down, the same way unrelated peoples elsewhere independently reached for other bitter yellow roots like goldenseal and Oregon grape. The Cherokee Nation, whose knowledge this comes from, published the Cherokee Phoenix in 1828, the first Native American newspaper, printed bilingually in Sequoyah's own syllabary.

name: Black Walnut Hull Wash
use: Ringworm and fungal skin problems
method: The green outer hull of black walnut was mashed into a pulp and rubbed on the rash.
note: The hull's dark, oily stain was itself taken as a rough sign of strength — folk logic held that a plant potent enough to stain skin for weeks was potent enough to fight a stubborn fungus too. Many Ozark and Appalachian settlers descended from Scots-Irish immigrants, whose isolation in these mountains preserved centuries-old British and Irish ballads that had already died out back in Britain — the same isolation that helped keep this kind of old-world folk medicine alive here too.
caution: Stains skin deeply for weeks and is not for broken or bleeding skin.

name: Dandelion Root Tonic
use: Digestion, liver complaints, “spring cleansing”
method: Autumn taproots were dug, roasted to deepen their flavor, and simmered into a dark tonic tea.
note: One of the classic Appalachian spring tonics, passed down largely by “granny women” who were often the only source of medical care available across huge stretches of the isolated backcountry, well into the 20th century in some hollows.

name: Mullein Leaf Tea
use: Cough, sore throat, chest congestion
method: The large velvety leaves were dried and steeped, always strained well through cloth to remove the fine irritating hairs before drinking.
note: So closely tied to lung complaints it earned the nickname “lungwort” in parts of Appalachia.

name: Horehound Candy & Tea
use: Cough, congestion, digestion
method: The bitter leaves were brewed into tea, or boiled down with sugar into hard candy that delivered the same dose in a form people actually wanted to take.
note: Horehound candy was once sold specifically as cough medicine disguised as a treat.

name: American Skullcap Tea
use: “Nerves,” sleeplessness, tension
method: The flowering herb was dried and steeped as a calming tea, or tinctured in spirits for a stronger, more concentrated dose.
note: A remedy like this was judged the old-fashioned way — by whether the person actually settled down and slept, repeated across a family over years, not by any chemical explanation. The Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution in 1827, with an elected principal chief, a two-house legislature, and a supreme court — a sophisticated government the U.S. dismantled through forced removal barely a decade later.

name: Wild Cherry Bark Syrup
use: Spasmodic cough
method: Inner bark was scraped from living branches and simmered gently with honey into a syrup, or preserved instead as a tincture in spirits for a remedy that kept through the whole winter.
note: Became a standard 19th-century American cough-syrup ingredient.
caution: Wilted leaves and improperly handled bark can release cyanide-related compounds — never use fallen or wilted material.

name: Black Cohosh Root
use: Menstrual and menopausal complaints, rheumatism
method: The dark root was decocted into a strong tea, or preserved as a tincture in spirits for a longer-lasting remedy.
note: An Indigenous women's medicine that entered mainstream American herbal practice and is still studied today.

name: American Ginseng Root
use: General weakness, fatigue, restorative tonic
method: The root was chewed fresh, decocted as a strengthening tonic, or preserved as a tincture in spirits.
note: Became so valuable that ginseng was one of colonial America's earliest exports to China, moving along the same Atlantic trade routes that carried tea and porcelain back the other way — and Appalachian families gathered and sold it commercially for generations after.

name: Broadleaf Plantain Poultice
people: European settlers, later adopted widely by Native nations
use: Insect bites, bee stings, splinters, minor wounds
method: Fresh ribbed leaves were picked, washed, and mashed or chewed into a wet green pulp, then bound over the skin with a clean cloth.
note: Nicknamed “the drawing leaf,” it traveled to America with European settlers and spread so readily along their trails that Indigenous nations came to call it “White Man's Footstep.”

name: Goldenseal Root Wash
use: Digestive, wound, and eye complaints
method: The yellow root was simmered into a decoction used as a wash or tonic, or preserved as a tincture in spirits for a stronger, more portable version.
note: Became one of the most commercially popular American roots — so popular that wild populations are now a conservation concern.
caution: Interacts with many prescription medicines and was historically used as an unsafe homemade eye wash.

name: Bear's Foot Poultice
use: Burns, cuts, swollen glands, back pain
method: Fresh leaves were crushed or chewed into a soft pulp and bound directly over the burn, cut, or swollen gland.
note: So little was recorded about exactly why bear's foot was chosen for these specific complaints that it stands as an honest reminder of how much old plant knowledge never made it into any written record — only the use survived, not always the reasoning behind it. Southeastern nations broadly descend from a deep agricultural and civic tradition stretching back to the Mississippian mound-building cultures.

name: Yellow Dock Root Tonic
use: Astringent, bowel complaints, “blood cleanser”
method: The root was dug, dried, and decocted into a bitter tonic.
note: Its deep bitterness marked it, in the old logic of “blood cleansers” and tonics, as a plant strong enough to work on the whole body at once. Plains nations who didn't share a spoken language also developed and shared Plains Indian Sign Language, a genuine lingua franca used for trade, storytelling, and diplomacy across an enormous stretch of the continent.

name: Lizard's Tail Root
use: Inflammation
method: The root was simmered into a decoction, or the fresh root pounded into a poultice and bound over the inflamed area.
note: Choosing a plant specifically for inflammation meant watching for a very physical, visible sign — swelling that had to go down — exactly the kind of clear, observable result that let old medicine get selected and passed on with real confidence.

name: Red Bay Leaf
use: Inflammation
method: Leaves were steeped into a strong tea, or crushed fresh and bound as a poultice over inflamed skin.
note: Its aromatic resemblance to the culinary bay leaf may be exactly why it got noticed and remembered as medicine in the first place — a familiar kitchen scent doing unfamiliar work. Antebellum New Orleans had one of the largest legally free Black and mixed-race populations anywhere in the South, the gens de couleur libres, who owned property and businesses under a level of legal standing almost unmatched elsewhere in the region at the time.

name: Groundsel Bush
use: General inflammatory and metabolic complaints
method: The leaves and bark were boiled down into a strong decoction, taken by the spoonful.
note: Reaching for a coastal shrub specifically for inflammation and metabolic complaints shows how closely old healers watched the body's own signals — swelling, sluggishness — and matched a plant to what they observed, long before anyone had a word like “metabolism.” Louisiana Creole is also a genuine, distinct language with its own grammar, not “broken French” as it was long dismissed.

name: Canada Goldenrod Tea
use: Digestive complaints, fever, liver complaints
method: The flowering herb was steeped into an infusion.
note: Goldenrod's bright, unmistakable yellow bloom made it easy to identify correctly every single year — no small thing when a mistaken plant could do real harm instead of good. Haudenosaunee clan mothers held real formal political power of their own — they alone had the authority to select a chief, and to remove one who failed his people, at a time when the European colonists arriving nearby granted women no comparable role in government.

name: Man-of-the-Earth Root
use: Digestive complaints, cough
method: The large underground root of this native morning-glory relative — genuinely massive, sometimes the size of a person's leg — was dug up and prepared as a decoction.
note: A root that size must have taken real effort to unearth, which says something about how much a Haudenosaunee family trusted it to be worth the work. The word Haudenosaunee itself means “people of the longhouse,” and their confederacy of six nations is considered by many historians one of the oldest continuously functioning participatory governments in the world.

name: Mouse-Ear Hawkweed
use: General infection-related complaints
method: The small flowering plant was steeped into a mild infusion.
note: Recorded in the same modern study that recreated several traditional Haudenosaunee water extracts to test them scientifically — proof that even the least famous plant in a well-documented tradition can still hold a real surprise.

name: White Sage / Prairie Sage
use: Pain, fever, respiratory and skin complaints, ceremony
method: Leaves were prepared as a smudge, a steam inhalation, or a simple infusion, depending on the purpose.
note: Its strong, immediately recognizable smell made it one of the easiest plants to identify with confidence, which may be part of why it was recorded for so many different purposes at once — over 240 documented uses in North American ethnobotanical records, more than almost any other plant.

name: Wild Bergamot Tea
use: Colds, cough, respiratory complaints
method: The aromatic flowering leaves were steeped as tea or used as a steam inhalation.
note: Its strong, oregano-like aroma was probably the whole reason it got noticed for colds in the first place — a smell sharp enough to feel like it was doing something the moment it was breathed in. Plains nations also engineered tipis specifically for the region's relentless wind, designed so two people could raise or strike one in under fifteen minutes.

name: Smooth Sumac Wash
use: Sore throat, mouth complaints, diarrhea, skin conditions
method: Berries, bark, and leaves were prepared as an astringent tea or wash.
note: In a modern lab screen of 100 Indigenous medicinal plants, smooth sumac was one of the few extracts active against every fungus tested — a rare case where the old, wide-ranging reputation and the modern lab result actually lined up.

name: Oshá Root
people: Rocky Mountain Indigenous nations & Hispanic communities
use: Colds, cough, sore throat, respiratory infection
method: The aromatic root was chewed directly or prepared as a tea or decoction.
note: Oshá's strong, celery-like smell and taste made it instantly recognizable to the people who relied on it, and that unmistakable identity is exactly why it stayed a trusted, specific remedy across generations rather than getting confused with anything else. Curanderismo, the broader Hispanic healing tradition oshá belongs to, carries influence stretching back through medieval Spain's centuries of Islamic rule, when Arabic medical scholarship deeply shaped Spanish folk practice.
caution: Oshá belongs to the carrot family, which includes deadly poisonous hemlock relatives — positive identification by an expert is essential.

name: Yerba Mansa Root
use: Wounds, infection, inflammation, respiratory complaints
method: Roots were simmered into a strong decoction for a wound wash, while fresh leaves were crushed into a poultice for infection or swelling.
note: Trusting a plant for wounds and infection came from watching, again and again, which injuries treated with it seemed to heal cleaner — the kind of patient, repeated observation that built real confidence over generations. Southwestern Pueblo peoples have inhabited villages like Acoma's “Sky City” continuously for close to a thousand years.

name: Northern Prickly Ash Bark
use: Toothache, digestive complaints, rheumatism
method: The bark was chewed directly against an aching tooth or prepared as a decoction.
note: Nicknamed the “toothache tree” — its numbing compounds explain why chewing the bark genuinely dulled pain, an immediate, unmistakable effect that made it easy to trust and remember.

name: Yerba Santa Tea
use: Cough, colds, asthma-like complaints, rheumatic pain
method: The resinous leaves were dried and steeped into tea, or chewed directly.
note: So respected for respiratory complaints that it was later stocked in mainstream 19th-century American pharmacies — a rare case of a California Indigenous remedy crossing directly into the settler drugstore.

name: Devil's Club Bark
use: Infection, arthritis, colds, diabetes-related complaints, general tonic
method: The inner bark was scraped — carefully, since the outer stalk is covered in sharp spines — and prepared as a decoction.
note: A plant this thorny and difficult to harvest safely wouldn't have stayed in use across generations unless people were genuinely convinced it was worth the trouble. Pacific Northwest nations also held potlatch ceremonies, elaborate feasts where status came from how much you gave away rather than how much you kept, a wealth system Canada banned outright from 1885 to 1951.

name: Oregon Grape Root
use: Stomach complaints, wounds, arthritis
method: The bright yellow root was decocted into a bitter tea or topical wash.
note: Contains the same berberine-family chemistry found in yellowroot and goldenseal, discovered independently on the opposite side of the continent — unrelated peoples, thousands of miles apart, separately noticing the same bitter yellow-root cure.

name: Labrador Tea
use: Respiratory and digestive complaints
method: The leathery leaves were steeped into an aromatic tea.
note: Its resinous, easy-to-identify leaves made it a plant people could gather with confidence in a landscape with few other options. “Alaska Native” covers genuinely distinct peoples — Iñupiat, Yupik, Unangax̂, Tlingit, Haida, and Athabaskan nations among others — each with their own separate languages and histories.
caution: Related Rhododendron species can be toxic, so correct identification matters.

name: High-Bush Cranberry
use: General nourishment and wellness
method: Berries were eaten fresh, dried, or cooked into preparations.
note: One of several far-northern berries where everyday food and medicine were essentially the same thing.

name: Salmonberry
use: General nourishment and wellness
method: Berries and young shoots were eaten fresh or preserved.
note: Like high-bush cranberry, valued as much for steady nutrition through the year as for treating any single complaint.

name: Corn Silk Tea
use: Urinary and kidney complaints
method: The fine golden threads from fresh corn were steeped into tea.
note: It was gentle and abundant enough — free with every harvest — to become one of the easiest remedies here to keep on hand, no special trip required. Everyday English words like chocolate, tomato, avocado, and coyote all come directly from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztec empire.

name: Estafiate Tea
use: Stomach pain, menstrual complaints, fever
method: The aromatic leaves were steeped as a tea.
note: Traditional curanderismo treats illness as having both a physical and a spiritual cause — susto (fright sickness), mal de ojo (evil eye) — a whole-person framework quite different from the purely physical model most of this archive otherwise reflects.
caution: This plant belongs to a genus with species-specific chemistry — correct identification matters before use.

name: Guava Leaf Tea
use: Diarrhea, stomach upset
method: Fresh or dried leaves were steeped into a strong tea.
note: One of the few folk digestive remedies with an actual randomized clinical trial behind it, showing reduced abdominal pain during diarrheal illness — an old household habit that held up when someone finally checked.

name: Senna Pod Tea
use: Occasional constipation
method: Dried pods or leaves were steeped into a mild tea.
note: One of the clearest folk-medicine success stories — its active compounds became the basis of modern stimulant laxatives.

name: Okra as Food-Medicine
use: Digestive support
method: Brought from West Africa and grown throughout the South, prepared as an everyday food rather than a separate medicine.
note: Okra itself is a direct West African crop, carried across the Atlantic in the transatlantic slave trade along with the deep agricultural knowledge of the people forced to grow it — knowledge that shaped Southern food and medicine far more than it's usually given credit for.

name: Cayenne Pepper Liniment
use: Sore muscles, cold stiff joints
method: Dried cayenne was simmered into melted lard and beeswax, then cooled into a rub-on liniment for aching joints.
note: Modern pain science confirms real chemistry behind this one — capsaicin remains an active ingredient in pain creams sold today.
caution: Wash hands thoroughly after handling, and keep well away from the eyes.

name: Turpentine Rub
use: Chest congestion, wounds, historically believed to treat worms
method: Pine-derived turpentine was rubbed on the chest or applied to wounds.
note: A once-common Southern household remedy.
caution: Turpentine is toxic if swallowed or inhaled in concentrated form and has no place in a modern medicine cabinet — historical interest only.

name: Slippery Elm Bark
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Sore throat, cough, digestive irritation
method: The inner bark was powdered and stirred into warm water and honey until it thickened into a soothing, slippery drink.
note: Its natural mucilage physically coats irritated tissue — a mechanism modern science still considers plausible, and one you could feel working the moment you swallowed it.

name: Willow Bark Tea
people: Woodland Indigenous nations & European settlers alike
use: Pain, fever, headaches, rheumatic aches
method: The green inner bark (cambium) was shaved from living willow branches and simmered into a bitter tea, or preserved as a tincture in spirits for a milder, more portable dose.
note: Willow bark contains salicin — the same chemical family later purified into aspirin. Two peoples an ocean apart, working independently, arrived at the same pain relief.

name: Wintergreen Leaf Tea
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Aches, pains, headaches
method: The glossy leaves were steeped into a minty tea, or crushed and rubbed directly on a sore spot.
note: Its oil is almost pure methyl salicylate — a close chemical cousin of the salicin in willow bark, discovered by an entirely different route.

name: Sweet Birch Tea
people: Indigenous nations & early settlers of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Aches and pains
method: The aromatic inner bark and twigs were steeped into a wintergreen-scented tea.
note: Tap the bark of a sweet birch in spring and the sap itself tastes of wintergreen — colonists used it to flavor medicine as often as to make it.

name: Mayapple Root
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Warts, and as a strong purgative
method: The root was dried and used in carefully measured small doses, or applied directly to warts.
note: One of American folk medicine's strangest legacies: this plant's toxic chemistry was eventually purified into podophyllotoxin, still used in wart treatments today and as a starting point for a family of cancer drugs.
caution: The plant is poisonous outside carefully controlled doses; only the ripe fruit is safely edible. Not a home remedy to attempt.

name: Feverfew Leaf
use: Headache
method: Fresh feverfew leaves were eaten plain or tucked between slices of bread, on the belief that chewing the bitter leaf itself eased head pain.
note: Eating the leaf directly, rather than brewing it, made this one of the few old remedies treated almost like food — the bitterness itself was the dose. Colonial almanacs doubled as medical references, often the only book besides the Bible in a household, packed with exactly this kind of advice.
caution: Chewing fresh leaves can cause mouth sores in some people.

name: Blackberry Root Decoction
use: Severe diarrhea, once called “summer complaint”
method: Woody roots were dug, scrubbed, chopped, and boiled down into a dark, astringent decoction, taken by the tablespoon through the day.
note: One of the most trusted cures for a diarrheal illness that was once a leading killer of children in hot weather — remembered as a battlefield remedy as well as a household one.
caution: Traditionally stopped the moment symptoms eased, to avoid swinging into severe constipation.

name: Comfrey (“Knitbone”) Poultice
use: Sprains, and bruised or broken bones
method: Roots and leaves were mashed into a thick green paste and packed directly over a splinted bone or wrapped joint, or preserved as a liniment in alcohol for the same external use.
note: Grown by nearly every German settler's barn specifically for this purpose — its old name, knitbone, says exactly what people believed it did.
caution: Never taken as a tea: comfrey contains compounds linked to serious liver damage when swallowed, and it was never applied to open or dirty wounds.

name: Arnica & St. John's Wort Oil
use: Bruises, sprains
method: Yellow arnica flowers or St. John's wort buds were infused for weeks in lard or oil, then rubbed gently into unbroken, bruised skin. St. John's wort in particular was just as often preserved instead as a drop-dosed tincture in spirits, taken for low spirits and nerve pain rather than rubbed on.
note: A German settler staple that made its way into Appalachian medicine chests as well.
caution: Never applied to broken skin or open wounds.

name: Wild Lettuce & Passionflower Tea
people: Cherokee & Creek nations, later country doctors
use: Pain, shock, sleeplessness
method: The bitter white sap of wild lettuce was collected and simmered into a dark syrup, or preserved as a tincture 19th-century doctors called lactucarium; dried passionflower leaves were steeped into a calming tea.
note: Wild lettuce earned the nickname “poor man's opium” for how it dulled pain and quieted the mind without the cost — or the addiction — of the real thing.
caution: Large amounts cause heavy drowsiness; not something to take before work requiring alertness.

name: Wild Onion Scalp Wash
use: Head lice, scalp fungus
method: Wild onion bulbs were crushed into a pulp and rubbed thoroughly into the hair and scalp, left twenty minutes, then rinsed clean.
note: An Appalachian homestead standby — the same sulfur compounds that make onions sting your eyes also made this wash work.

name: Stinging Nettle & Basswood Hair Rinse
use: Thinning hair, dandruff
method: Dried nettle and basswood leaves were boiled into a dark tea, cooled completely, and poured over the hair as a final rinse.
note: Boiling or drying nettle completely removes its sting, leaving behind only the plant's silica and soothing mucilage — a way of taming a plant that fights back into something safe to use. The Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) are among the largest Native nations in North America today, with communities spanning from the Great Lakes deep into Canada.

name: Nettle Whipping for Arthritis
people: Settlers and Native hunters across many regions
use: Arthritis and rheumatism in stiff, painful joints
method: Live stinging nettle was gathered fresh and deliberately brushed or "whipped" directly across an aching joint, left unwashed and uncooked so the sting stayed intact.
note: Fighting pain with more pain wasn't as strange as it sounds — deliberately irritating the skin over a joint is a genuinely old pain-relief trick, and modern topical arthritis treatments still work on the same basic principle of overriding one sensation with another.
caution: Used only externally and briefly, on unbroken skin — the same fresh sting causes real burns and blistering if overdone.

name: Osha Root
people: Rocky Mountain Indigenous nations & Hispanic communities of the Southwest
use: Colds, cough, and sore throat
method: The root was chewed directly, or brewed into a tea or decoction.
note: Osha's reputation as a reliable cold-and-cough remedy runs deep enough that it's still commercially wildcrafted today — yet, oddly, real clinical trials on the plant itself remain sparse even now.
caution: Osha root closely resembles deadly poison hemlock when growing wild, and misidentification during harvest has caused fatal poisonings.

name: Goldthread
use: Mouth sores, sore throat, and digestive complaints
method: The thread-thin yellow rhizome was chewed directly, or brewed into an infusion used as a mouth wash.
note: Its common nickname, "canker root," comes directly from this exact traditional use against mouth sores — the name and the remedy grew up together.
caution: Its concentrated alkaloids can interact with other medicines and were traditionally avoided during pregnancy.

name: Partridgeberry
people: Indigenous midwifery traditions of the Northeast
use: Support during pregnancy and childbirth
method: The trailing evergreen vine's leaves were steeped into an infusion, traditionally given to women in the weeks before labor.
note: It was historically passed along specifically among midwives and women healers rather than kept as ordinary household medicine — a specialist's plant, not a general one.
caution: Historically used only under a midwife's direct guidance in the final weeks of pregnancy, never as a casual home remedy.

name: Chokecherry
use: A food-medicine for digestive and respiratory complaints
method: The fruit was eaten fresh, dried, or pounded into pemmican, while the bark was occasionally simmered into a decoction.
note: Chokecherry shares its cyanide-precursor chemistry with wild cherry and peach — plants with completely different common names, but close cousins in the very same genus.
caution: The seeds and bark contain compounds that release cyanide; historical preparation always meant removing or avoiding the pits, never eating them.

name: Lemon Beebalm Tea
use: Fever, cough, and colds
method: The lemon-scented leaves and flowering tops were steeped into a hot tea.
note: Its essential oil runs unusually rich in thymol, the same aromatic compound that gives common culinary thyme its bite — the Plains had their own homegrown answer to a European kitchen herb.
caution: The concentrated essential oil can irritate skin and mucous membranes; historical use was a mild tea, never a strong extract.

name: Canada Yew Tea
use: Rheumatism
method: The needles were steeped into a tea taken internally, or used in a sweat bath, depending on the community.
note: Yew's chemistry was eventually linked to the taxane family — the same class of compound behind the cancer drug paclitaxel, though traditional yew tea and purified modern chemotherapy are worlds apart in practice.
caution: Yew foliage and seeds are genuinely poisonous. This is preserved here as documented history only, not something to prepare.

name: Speckled Alder
use: Wounds, severe fever, sore eyes, and a spring cleansing purge
method: The bark was scraped and boiled for a wound wash, whole leaves were wrapped directly around the body for fever, a bark decoction was used to bathe sore eyes, and the same bark, boiled stronger, served as a seasonal purge.
note: One shrub, four completely different jobs — the Mi'kmaq, Woods Cree, and Seneca each found a different use for the same plant, a reminder of how differently the same forest could be read by different nations.
caution: The eye-wash and internal purge uses carry real risk of contamination or overuse and are preserved here as history only.

name: Eastern Hemlock Bark Tea
people: Ojibwe, Maliseet, Mi'kmaq, Cherokee, Potawatomi, Abenaki, Algonquin, Seneca & Delaware nations
use: Diarrhea and rheumatism
method: The red inner bark was brewed into an astringent tonic for the stomach, or the foliage steeped into an infusion taken for aching joints.
note: This tree is one of the leading candidates for "annedda," the mystery tree whose bark tea cured Jacques Cartier's scurvy-stricken crew in the winter of 1535-36 — one of the earliest recorded moments of European explorers surviving only because of Indigenous plant knowledge.
caution: This tree (Tsuga canadensis) is completely unrelated to poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) or water hemlock (Cicuta) — both deadly — despite sharing the common name "hemlock."

name: Spanish Moss Fever Remedy
people: Houma nation & other Gulf South communities
use: Chills, fever, catarrh, and asthma
method: The moss was decocted as a fever remedy, or used in a sweat-inducing bath to treat congestion.
note: The same moss that went into a sickbed remedy also went into the bed itself — Spanish moss was a standard mattress stuffing and cordage material across the Gulf South, moving constantly between medicine chest and household material.
caution: Wild Spanish moss can harbor insects and debris and shouldn't be assumed clean without real preparation.

name: Ground Juniper Respiratory Tea
people: Mi'kmaq, Maliseet, Cayuga, Ojibwe & Woods Cree nations
use: Lung and respiratory disorders, including colds, asthma, and tuberculosis
method: The plant was decocted and drunk, though the exact part used and specific indication varied by nation.
note: Juniper shows up as a respiratory remedy again and again among northern nations who otherwise had little contact with each other — the same evergreen, independently reached for, hundreds of miles apart.
caution: Concentrated juniper preparations can irritate the kidneys and digestive tract, and were considered unsafe during pregnancy.

name: Black Sage Leaf Remedies
use: Gas pains, earache, cough, heart complaints, paralysis, sore throat, and chronic bronchial cough
method: Leaves were chewed directly, or made into a poultice, infusion, decoction, or bath, depending on the specific complaint.
note: Black sage was a genuine multi-tool plant for California coastal nations — the Costanoan alone are documented using five completely different preparation methods for five completely different ailments from the same shrub.
caution: The concentrated essential oil is far stronger than a traditional leaf preparation and can irritate or be toxic — this describes the mild traditional forms only.

name: Hoof Fungus Rheumatism Treatment
use: Rheumatism and joint pain
method: A piece of the fungus was pounded soft, placed directly over the painful joint, and set alight, burning slowly down toward the skin like a coal.
note: This is genuinely different from the settler use of the same fungus as fire-starting tinder — here the fungus itself becomes the treatment, used almost exactly like moxibustion, a controlled-burn therapy independently developed continents apart.
caution: This controlled-burn method causes real burns by design and carries a real risk of infection — preserved here as documented history only.

name: Lowbush Blueberry Medicine
use: Gastrointestinal complaints, gynecological complaints, and as a blood medicine
method: Beyond simply eating the berries as food, the plant was separately prepared as a medicinal decoction for specific complaints.
note: The same plant lived two lives — the everyday food eaten straight off the bush, and a completely separate medicinal preparation reserved for specific ailments, including a documented role in Iroquois ceremonial medicine.

name: Puffball for Sheep Bone Fractures
use: Setting broken bones in sheep and other livestock
method: The puffball's spore powder was applied to a sheep's broken leg bone as part of setting and treating the fracture.
note: Not every historical remedy here was for people — sheep were the literal backbone of Navajo pastoral life, and this shows the same puffball-spore-as-medicine logic extended to livestock care, not just human wounds.

name: American Beautyberry Root Sweat Bath
use: Rheumatism, fever, colic, and dysentery
method: The root and branches were decocted and used both in a sweat bath for rheumatism and fever, and taken internally for colic and digestive complaints.
note: The same shrub Southern gardeners now grow for its purple berries did double duty as both a steam-bath medicine and an internal remedy — a very different job from its other documented use as an insect repellent.
caution: The sweat-bath method carries real risk of overheating and dehydration, and malaria-associated fever always needs real medical treatment.

name: Sweetgum Resin Salve & Tea
use: Diarrhea, dysentery, anxiety, and skin wounds
method: The bark was steeped into a tea taken internally for digestive complaints and anxiety, while the tree's own resin was mixed with rendered tallow into a topical salve for cuts, sores, and wounds.
note: Anxiety sits right alongside diarrhea and open wounds on the list of what this tree treated — a reminder that Cherokee medicine didn't draw the same hard line between physical and mental complaints that modern medicine does.
caution: A nonsterile resin salve carries real contamination risk on open wounds, and serious diarrhea needs real hydration and medical care.

name: Flowering Dogwood Root & Bark Medicine
use: Headache, fever, body aches, and as a general tonic
method: The bark was chewed directly for headache, or decocted into a tea taken for fever and as a tonic; the root was also prepared separately as a tonic.
note: This is a separate tradition from the well-known settler use of dogwood bark as a quinine substitute — dogwood was already established fever medicine among Southeastern and Gulf nations well before settlers picked it up.
caution: Large doses can cause nausea, and using dogwood in place of real fever or malaria treatment carries real risk.

name: Black Walnut Bark Medicine
use: As a cathartic, an emetic, and for toothache
method: The inner bark was steeped into a strong tea taken to induce vomiting or purging, or chewed directly and held against an aching tooth.
note: This internal, purgative use of black walnut bark is a genuinely different tradition from the external antifungal wash better known among Appalachian settlers — same tree, same bark, two very different medicine cabinets.
caution: The bark is genuinely potent — induced vomiting and purging both carry real risk, and this is documented history only.

name: Cherokee Sassafras Medicine
use: Spider bites, scrofula, sprains, bruises, and sore or infected eyes
method: Leaves and bark were chewed and the juice spat directly onto a spider bite, while the root was brewed into a tea for internal complaints like scrofula.
note: This Cherokee tradition is distinct from the famous settler "spring tonic" use of sassafras — the same root, but a completely different set of specific ailments, including direct first-aid use on a fresh bite.
caution: Sassafras root contains safrole, now recognized as a liver toxin, and conditions like scrofula and infected spider bites need real medical treatment.

name: Red Mulberry Root & Bark
use: Urinary complaints, ringworm, and constipation
method: The root was prepared as a medicinal extract for urinary complaints, the sap rubbed directly onto ringworm patches, and the bark steeped into a laxative tea.
note: Three completely different parts of the same familiar fruit tree — root, sap, and bark — each carried its own separate medicinal job among different Southeastern nations.
caution: Bark preparations used as a laxative carry a real dehydration risk if overdone.

name: Oak Gall Eye Remedy
use: Eye problems
note: A wasp-induced gall on the oak tree was ground to powder and mixed with water — real, but only a single thin record with no further detail on dosage or exact ailment.

name: Oak Bark Cough Remedy
use: Cough
note: Named in the research as a Miwok cough remedy using a bark mixture, but with no further preparation detail given.

name: Red Oak for Heart Problems
use: Heart problems
note: Named in the research alongside red oak's non-medicinal uses (sacred fire wood, basketry, food), but with no specific preparation method documented for this particular use.

name: Andrographis
people: Apatani people of the Ziro Valley, Arunachal Pradesh, India
use: A bitter herb used as an anti-inflammatory and immune remedy in Apatani ethnobotanical medicine
note: Turned up in research covering a 158-species Apatani (India) ethnobotanical survey. This is an Indian Himalayan tradition with no documented American community or historical use — kept here for transparency about what the research considered.

name: Gotu Kola
people: Apatani people of India, and broader South/Southeast Asian Ayurvedic tradition
use: Leaves used for wound healing, skin complaints, and as a cognitive tonic in Ayurvedic and Apatani ethnobotanical medicine
note: A well-known Ayurvedic and Southeast Asian herb that surfaced repeatedly in the research as a 'gold star' candidate, but with no documented American immigrant-community adoption — included for transparency rather than silently dropped.

name: Ageratum
people: Pantropical folk tradition — African, Asian, and Latin American communities, and named in Apatani (India) ethnobotanical research
use: A common pantropical weed used across African, Asian, and Latin American folk medicine
note: No U.S. settler or Indigenous adoption of this specific plant is documented in the sources reviewed; kept visible as a considered-but-out-of-scope item.

name: Black Seed
people: Middle Eastern and South Asian Islamic and Ayurvedic medicine tradition
use: Seeds used as a bitter digestive and general-wellness remedy in Middle Eastern and South Asian traditional medicine
note: Repeatedly flagged in the research as a promising plant, but no historical U.S. community or usage story is documented — kept for transparency, not as an American remedy.

name: Boswellia (Frankincense)
people: Ayurvedic and Middle Eastern/Islamic medicine tradition; the resin was also burned in some American Catholic devotional contexts
use: Resin used as a traditional anti-inflammatory remedy in South Asian and Middle Eastern medicine, and burned as incense
note: A recurring 'gold star' research candidate with no documented American folk-medicine use of its own — its only American presence is as devotional incense, not a home remedy.

name: Devil's Claw
use: Root used as a traditional anti-inflammatory and pain remedy in Southern Africa
note: A real, well-documented Southern African plant with no U.S. historical use mentioned anywhere in the research reviewed — included for transparency about what was considered and rejected as out of scope.

name: Turmeric
people: Ayurvedic, Traditional Chinese, and Islamic medicine traditions
use: Root used as a digestive and anti-inflammatory remedy across South Asian, Chinese, and Middle Eastern traditional medicine
note: Came up across several research passes as a modern liver-protective research subject, but no U.S. community or historical preparation method is documented — a global spice with no American folk-remedy story of its own in this archive's window.

name: Artichoke Leaf
people: Modern hepatoprotective research subject; also simply grown and eaten as a vegetable in American households
use: Leaf extract studied in modern research for liver support; the plant itself is mostly just a garden vegetable in America
note: No documented specific American folk-medicine story beyond being eaten — included for transparency since it appeared repeatedly in the research as a liver-health candidate.

name: Schisandra
use: Berry used as a liver-protective and restorative tonic in Traditional Chinese medicine
note: Discussed only as a modern hepatoprotective research subject with no documented use by Chinese-American herbalists or households in the sources reviewed.

name: Sea Buckthorn
people: Modern commercial supplement and skincare trade; historically a Eurasian folk plant
use: Berries and oil used as a modern wellness supplement; no historical American folk tradition documented
note: A Eurasian plant with real folk-medicine roots in Scandinavia and Russia, but its American presence is a purely modern commercial-supplement phenomenon, not a rooted household remedy — kept visible rather than silently dropped.

name: Reishi Mushroom
use: A polypore mushroom used as a general tonic in East Asian traditional medicine
note: Reishi's documented medicinal tradition is East Asian; no American folk-medicine adoption story is documented in the sources reviewed, unlike the related American 'reishi' marketing name which has no period historical use at all.

name: Split Gill Mushroom
use: A common wood-decay fungus with documented traditional medicinal use in Africa and Asia
note: No American historical use of this fungus was found in the research reviewed — included for transparency about what was considered.

name: Galangal
people: Southeast Asian and Traditional Chinese medicine
use: Rhizome used as a digestive and anti-inflammatory remedy in Southeast Asian and Chinese medicine
note: A non-U.S.-origin root with no documented adoption into American folk practice in this archive's historical window — kept visible for transparency.

name: Copal Resin
people: Mexican and Mexican-American curanderismo and botánica tradition
use: Resin burned for spiritual cleansing and protection in curanderismo and botánica practice
note: A real ceremonial resin, but its documented American use reads as a modern (20th-century-onward) botánica practice rather than a clear fit for this archive's older historical window — included rather than dropped.

name: Quinoa
use: A grain domesticated in the Andes and eaten as a staple food
note: An Andean domesticate with no historical American use in this archive's period — its U.S. popularity is a very modern (late-20th-century) health-food phenomenon.

name: Tomatillo
people: Mesoamerican food tradition, carried into Mexican-American cooking
use: A Mesoamerican food domesticate used in cooking; no specific U.S.-community medicinal documentation found
note: Distinct from the wild Plains 'wild tomatillo' already noted elsewhere in the research — this is the cultivated Mesoamerican food plant, included here as food-only, not a documented remedy.

name: Sotol
people: Southwestern Indigenous nations and Mexican-American communities
use: Heart of the plant roasted for food and fermented into a traditional liquor; leaves used for basketry
note: Primarily documented as a food, beverage, and fiber/basketry material rather than a medicine — kept visible as household/practical history.

name: Beargrass
use: Leaves used as a fiber material for basketry
note: Primarily documented as a basketry and fiber material rather than a medicine — kept visible as household/practical history.

name: Psyllium
people: Persian and South Asian traditional medicine; a modern American commercial fiber-supplement ingredient
use: Seed husk used as a bulk laxative in Persian and South Asian traditional medicine, and sold today as a commercial fiber supplement
note: A non-U.S.-origin plant with no documented historical American folk use; the related native common plantain already has its own entry in the archive and fills a similar niche.

name: Rock Tripe
people: Documented mainly through Canadian Arctic exploration narratives (the Franklin expeditions), rather than a specific U.S. Indigenous community
use: A famine food ('tripe de roche') eaten by explorers and northern peoples when other food ran out
note: A genuine famine-food lichen, but its strongest documented record is Canadian Arctic exploration history rather than a specific U.S. Indigenous community's remedy — too thin to confidently attribute to a U.S. tradition, kept visible regardless.

name: Groundnut
people: Wampanoag and other Eastern Woodlands nations; famous as a Pilgrim survival food
use: Tubers eaten as a critical wild food, including by starving Plymouth colonists in their first winters
note: A celebrated food plant with no documented medicinal angle found in the research — included as food-only history rather than dropped.

name: Beach Plum
people: Northeastern coastal Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Fruit eaten fresh and preserved as jam along the Atlantic coast
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use, kept here for completeness.

name: Chickasaw Plum
people: Southeastern Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Fruit eaten fresh and preserved
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: American Plum
people: Plains and Midwestern Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Fruit eaten fresh, dried, and preserved
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Gooseberry
people: Northeastern and Great Lakes Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Fruit eaten fresh and preserved
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Cloudberry
people: Alaska Native and northern New England communities
use: Fruit gathered and eaten, especially in northern bogs and tundra
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use, though it is a genuinely prized northern food plant.

name: Marsh Marigold
people: Eastern Indigenous nations and settler households ('cowslip greens')
use: Cooked spring greens, eaten after boiling to remove natural toxins
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — the raw plant is mildly toxic and must be cooked, but no medicinal use is documented.

name: Alkali Sacaton
use: Seed grain gathered as food in arid grasslands
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Whipple Cholla
use: Flower buds and fruit eaten as food, like other cholla cactus
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Allegheny Chinquapin
people: Southeastern Indigenous nations and Appalachian settler households
use: Small chestnut-like nuts gathered and eaten
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Pecan
people: Southeastern and Southern Plains Indigenous nations, later a major American food crop
use: Nuts gathered and eaten as a staple food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use, despite its major importance in American foodways.

name: Buffaloberry
use: Berries eaten fresh and whipped into a foamy dessert, similar to the related soapberry
note: A real Plains food plant, related to but a distinct species from the already-documented Soapberry — no medicinal use beyond food/beverage could be confirmed.

name: American Hazelnut
people: Eastern Woodlands Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Nuts gathered and eaten
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Beaked Hazelnut
people: Great Lakes and Northern Indigenous nations
use: Nuts gathered and eaten
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Palo Verde
use: Seeds gathered and eaten as a food source in the desert
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Singleleaf Pinyon
use: Pine nuts gathered as a critical staple food; pitch also used generically for wounds
note: An essential Great Basin food staple; its wound-pitch use is generic and already well represented by other pine-pitch entries, but the food role itself is real and distinct enough to note here.

name: Pacific Crabapple
use: Fruit stored in grease or made into preserves
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Southern Crabapple
people: Southeastern Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Fruit made into jelly and preserves
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Greasewood Ash
people: Southwestern Indigenous nations, including the Hopi
use: Burned to ash and used as a mordant/leavening additive in blue cornmeal food preparation
note: A real, specific food-processing use, but not a medicinal remedy — included as documented material-culture history.

name: American Lotus
use: Tubers and seeds eaten as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Arrow Arum
use: Root processed into 'tuckahoe' bread, a documented Chesapeake food staple
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use, but a specific and well-attested Chesapeake foodway worth keeping visible.

name: Jerusalem Artichoke
people: Eastern Woodlands Indigenous nations, later a major American food crop
use: Tubers gathered and cultivated as a major food staple
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Silverweed
use: Root cultivated and eaten as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Hog Peanut
use: Underground seed gathered as a supplementary food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use.

name: Yampah
people: Western Indigenous nations of the Great Basin and Rockies
use: Root gathered as a major staple food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented medicinal use, despite its major dietary importance.

name: Lamb's Quarters
people: Indigenous nations and settler households across many regions
use: Wild potherb greens gathered and cooked as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented specific medicinal use beyond being a nourishing wild green.

name: Good King Henry
use: Wild/cultivated potherb greens brought from Old World gardening tradition
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented specific medicinal use.

name: Pigweed (Amaranth)
people: Southwestern Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Wild greens and grain gathered and eaten as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no documented specific medicinal use.

name: Great Camas
use: Bulb roasted and eaten as a major staple food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — an important staple food, but no documented medicinal use.

name: Wapato
people: Columbia River and other Western Indigenous nations
use: Tuber gathered and eaten as a major staple food, documented in the Lewis and Clark journals
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — a well-documented staple food, but no medicinal angle.

name: Bitterroot
people: Interior Northwest Indigenous nations, especially the Salish (the plant is the namesake of Montana's Bitterroot Valley)
use: Root cooked and eaten as a profoundly important food and trade staple, also used ceremonially
note: Its primary documented role is as a food and trade staple rather than a medicine — a genuine medicinal (not food) use is too thin to responsibly write as fact, but its cultural importance made it worth keeping visible.

name: Pickerelweed
use: Young leaves and seeds eaten as a minor wild food
note: Only a minor, thin food use is documented, with no medicinal angle — kept here rather than dropped entirely.

name: American Vetch
use: Seeds and shoots used as a minor food, with uncertain minor medicinal use also recalled
note: Only thin, uncertain recall of a minor food and possible medicinal use — included for completeness despite the weak sourcing.

name: Johnny-Jump-Up
people: European immigrant households, carrying the Old World 'heartsease' tradition
use: Flowers and leaves used in European 'heartsease' folk tradition for heart and emotional complaints
note: A close relative of the already-noted native Violet (Viola sororia); no confident, distinctly American adoption story is documented beyond general Old World lore carried by immigrant households.

name: Inkberry
use: Leaves possibly used, like Yaupon Holly, as a 'black drink' caffeinated ceremonial tea
note: A relative of Yaupon Holly with a possible but not confidently distinguishable 'black drink' tradition of its own — kept visible as a related, thinner lead.

name: Possumhaw
use: Possibly used, like Yaupon Holly, as a tea-substitute plant
note: A relative of Yaupon Holly with a possible but not confidently distinguishable tea tradition of its own — kept visible as a related, thinner lead.

name: Deerbrush
people: California and Pacific Northwest Indigenous nations
use: Branches used as a soap substitute and basketry material
note: Best documented as a material-culture plant (soap, basketry) rather than a medicine — included as household/practical history.

name: Ocean Spray
use: Extremely hard wood ('ironwood') used to make tools, arrow shafts, and digging implements
note: A material-culture entry rather than a medicine — its documented importance is as a tool-making hardwood, kept visible for completeness.

name: Wild Columbine
use: Seeds rubbed on the hands as a love-charm and perfume to attract a suitor
note: A genuine documented courtship-charm practice rather than a remedy for illness, so it didn't fit the archive's medicine focus even though the underlying fact is real — included since the user wants this kind of 'inappropriate for strict medicine scope' item visible rather than dropped.

name: Silverleaf Nightshade
use: Berries used as a rennet substitute in traditional cheesemaking
note: A food-technology use (cheesemaking), not a medicine — its edible parts are otherwise toxic, so this is a specific, narrow practical use rather than a home remedy.

name: Lemonade Berry
people: Southern California Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Berries soaked in water to make a tart beverage
note: A beverage-only use as far as the research could confirm — no confident specific medicinal documentation.

name: Muscadine Grape
people: Southeastern Indigenous nations and settler households
use: Fruit eaten fresh and made into wine
note: Well documented as food and wine, with no confident specific medicinal-folk detail beyond generic tonic use.

name: Watercress
people: American settler households, part of general spring-greens foraging
use: Gathered as an early-spring wild green, eaten for a tonic effect after a winter diet
note: Very similar to the already-documented Wintercress spring-tonic tradition; likely part of the same general foraging practice rather than a clean, distinct entry, but kept visible as its own named plant.

name: Peppergrass
people: Southern rural households, including a documented Civil War-era pepper-substitute use
use: Leaves used as a pepper substitute and gathered as 'creasy greens' in early spring
note: Overlaps with the Wintercress spring-greens tradition, but has its own specific Civil War-era pepper-substitute story worth keeping visible.

name: Royal Jelly
use: A beekeeping product taken as a general health tonic
note: A real product with a genuine following, but its American popularity is a mid-20th-century health-food-store phenomenon, outside this archive's usual historical window — kept visible as a modern commodity considered during research.

name: Nutritional Yeast
use: Deactivated yeast flakes eaten as a vitamin and general-health supplement
note: A later 20th-century health-food-store product, distinct in era from the archive's already-included 19th/early-20th-century Fleischmann's Yeast Cakes entry — kept visible as a modern commodity the research considered.

name: Limewater
people: American households following pediatrician L. Emmett Holt's widely-followed infant-feeding guidance, late 19th/early 20th century
use: Mixed into infant formula to help settle a baby's digestion
note: A real, documented late-19th/early-20th-century practice, but it leans clinical/advice-manual rather than folk tradition, and shares a base ingredient with the archive's already-included 'Carron Oil' burn remedy — kept as its own entry since the use (infant feeding) is genuinely distinct.

name: Beef Tea (Bone Broth)
people: American households, following period cookery and invalid-care manuals
use: Broth made by simmering beef bones and meat, given to the sick and convalescent for strength
note: A real, well-documented sickroom food that overlaps thematically with the archive's already-included Calf's Foot Jelly entry, but is a distinctly different, separately-named preparation worth keeping visible.

name: Peanut Oil Massage (Carver's Polio Treatment)
people: George Washington Carver, promoted to the American public, 1930s
use: Peanut oil massage promoted by Carver as a treatment for polio-related muscle weakness
note: A real, famous historical episode, but it was an actively promoted, unproven health claim from the 1930s rather than a rooted folk tradition, and falls slightly outside the archive's usual earlier historical window — kept visible rather than dropped for being 'inappropriate' as an unproven medical claim.

name: Poison Ivy
people: Documented in old American medical records as an experimental irritant, and in homeopathic 'Rhus tox' preparations
use: Historically tested as an irritant/counter-irritant in old medical records and used in tiny homeopathic doses for rheumatic complaints
note: Its only real historical significance is as a plant people worked hard to avoid, not a genuine home remedy — kept visible with a clear warning rather than silently dropped.
caution: Causes severe allergic contact dermatitis (urushiol) in the great majority of people who touch it. This entry documents historical curiosity only — never handle, burn, or apply poison ivy in any form.

name: Kentucky Coffeetree Seeds
people: Pioneer households, used as a coffee substitute when real coffee was unavailable
use: Roasted seeds used as a pioneer-era coffee substitute
note: A real frontier practice, but the raw and improperly-roasted seeds and pods are toxic — no confident, specific medicinal-remedy detail exists beyond this risky coffee substitute.
caution: The raw seeds and pods contain toxic compounds (cytisine-like alkaloids) and are unsafe unless thoroughly roasted; historically, improperly prepared seeds caused poisoning. Documented as history only, not a recommendation.

name: Dutchman's Breeches
people: Documented mainly as a livestock hazard on American farms
use: Known historically mainly as a poisonous plant causing 'staggers' in grazing livestock, not as a human remedy
note: Thin remedy evidence exists at all — its real historical significance is as a recognized poison, kept visible with a clear warning rather than dropped.
caution: Contains isoquinoline alkaloids that are toxic if ingested, historically causing tremors and 'staggers' in livestock. Not a safe home remedy in any form.

name: Baneberry
people: Recognized and avoided across many Eastern Woodlands communities and settler households
use: Historically known and avoided as a dangerously poisonous plant ('doll's eyes'), not used as a remedy
note: Genuinely dangerous rather than medicinal — the user asked for dangerous plants to be flagged rather than omitted, so this is kept visible with a clear warning.
caution: All parts of the plant, especially the berries, are highly toxic and can cause cardiac symptoms if eaten. This is documented as a recognized poison only — never ingest any part of this plant.

name: Fly Agaric Mushroom
people: Documented in general American mycological/folk knowledge as a toxic and psychoactive mushroom
use: Historically recognized as a toxic, psychoactive mushroom rather than a remedy
note: Included for transparency about the research's scope, with a clear safety warning rather than being silently omitted.
caution: Contains toxic and psychoactive compounds (muscimol, ibotenic acid) that cause serious illness and can be fatal, especially if misidentified. Never eat this mushroom.

name: Destroying Angel Mushroom
people: Documented in American mycological history as one of the deadliest wild mushrooms
use: Not a remedy of any kind — historically significant only as a lethal poisonous mushroom, frequently fatally confused with edible species
note: Genuinely dangerous, not a home remedy — included with a strong warning per the user's request that dangerous items be flagged rather than deleted.
caution: One of the deadliest mushrooms in North America; ingestion causes fatal liver and kidney failure and there is no reliable folk antidote. Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification.

name: Moonseed
people: Recognized and avoided by foragers as a toxic wild-grape lookalike
use: Chiefly notable as a poisonous vine easily confused with true wild grapes, not as a remedy
note: Remedy evidence is too thin to responsibly feature as medicine — its real significance is as a recognized danger, kept visible with a warning.
caution: The berries closely resemble wild grapes but contain toxic alkaloids; ingestion can cause serious poisoning. Never eat unless positively identified by an expert.

name: Death Camas
people: Western Indigenous nations, who worked hard to distinguish it from the edible camas root it closely resembles
use: Not a remedy — historically significant as a deadly poison that Indigenous root-gatherers had to carefully avoid while harvesting edible camas
note: Its only real historical significance is as a dangerous poison, not a documented healing use — included per the user's request that dangerous plants be flagged clearly rather than silently omitted.
caution: All parts of this plant are highly toxic and can be fatal if ingested; it closely resembles the edible camas lily and has caused fatal poisonings from misidentification. Never eat any part of this plant.

name: California Pipevine (Birthwort)
use: Root historically used medicinally by some California Indigenous communities, in the same family as the archive's Virginia Snakeroot
note: A different species from the already-documented Virginia Snakeroot, with real historical use but also a serious, now well-understood modern safety concern — kept visible with a clear warning.
caution: Aristolochia species contain aristolochic acid, now recognized as a potent kidney toxin and carcinogen. Documented as historical use only — this plant should not be used medicinally.

name: Pomegranate Root Bark
people: 19th-century American medicine, drawn from a long Old World tradition
use: Root bark decoction historically used as a tapeworm remedy
note: A real 19th-century American medicinal use, distinct from the archive's already-included pomegranate rind tea (a different plant part, used for diarrhea) — the root-bark anthelmintic dose carried real risk, so it's flagged here.
caution: The alkaloid (pelletierine) that made root-bark tea effective against tapeworms is also toxic in excess and historically caused dangerous side effects at the doses needed to work. Documented as history only.

name: Cannabis (Hemp) Tincture
people: American pharmacies and patent-medicine makers, 19th century
use: A tincture made from the flowering tops, official in the U.S. Pharmacopeia and sold for pain, spasms, and sleeplessness
note: A genuine, well-documented 19th-century American pharmacy item — distinct from the modern hemp-seed-oil product sometimes mistakenly linked to this history, which was not the actual historical medicine.
caution: Historical tincture dosing was highly unpredictable and cannabis is a controlled substance today; this entry documents 19th-century pharmacy history only, not a usable or legal remedy.

name: Psilocybin Mushrooms
people: Mazatec ceremonial tradition (Mexico), with 20th-century American cultural engagement
use: Used ceremonially in Mazatec healing tradition; American engagement with this practice is a 20th-century phenomenon
note: A real and culturally significant tradition, but it's a Mesoamerican (Mazatec) practice rather than a U.S. household remedy, and American interest in it postdates this archive's usual historical window — included for transparency with a clear caution.
caution: A controlled substance with real psychological risks, especially from misidentification of wild mushrooms. Documented as cultural history only, not a usable home remedy.

name: Artist's Conk
use: The smooth underside of this bracket fungus was etched with a fine point and used as a folk-art 'canvas'
note: Known mainly for this craft use, not as a medicine — no confident historical American remedy record was found.

name: Dryad's Saddle
use: A wild mushroom eaten for its distinctive watermelon-rind flavor when young
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: Oyster Mushroom
use: A common wild mushroom gathered and eaten as food
