note: Food-only historically — modern lab bioactivity research isn't the same as documented historical folk medicine.

name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
use: A distinctive wild mushroom eaten as food
note: Food-only historically; its modern reputation as a nerve/nootropic supplement is a 21st-century phenomenon, not period folk use.

name: Maitake (Hen of the Woods)
use: A prized wild mushroom gathered and eaten by Italian-American and Appalachian foragers
note: A real and specific foraging tradition; its separate Japanese medicinal reputation is not documented as having transferred into American use.

name: Berkeley's Polypore
use: A minor wild mushroom gathered and eaten as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: Cauliflower Mushroom
use: A choice wild edible mushroom gathered and eaten as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: Shaggy Mane Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom eaten as food while young; its inky, self-dissolving cap was also sometimes used as a curiosity ink
note: Food-only historically, with a fun craft-curiosity detail (ink); not confidently documented as a specific American remedy.

name: Morel Mushroom
use: A highly prized wild mushroom gathered every spring, especially across the Midwest
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found, despite its major foraging-culture importance.

name: Lobster Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom prized as food for its color and texture
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: Blewit Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom carried into American use by European-immigrant foraging tradition
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: King Bolete (Porcini)
use: A prized wild mushroom central to Italian-American foraging tradition
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found, despite major foraging-culture importance.

name: Matsutake Mushroom
use: A highly prized wild mushroom central to Japanese-American Pacific Northwest foraging culture
note: Food and economic use only — no medicinal record was found, though the foraging tradition itself is well documented and worth keeping visible.

name: Saffron Milkcap Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom carried into American use by European-immigrant foraging tradition
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: Russula Mushrooms
use: A large, variable-quality genus of wild mushrooms gathered by foragers
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no medicinal record found.

name: Dulse (Pacific)
use: A red seaweed dried and eaten as food
note: The Pacific species, distinct from the Atlantic species behind the well-known Irish-American dulse-eating tradition — food-only, no confident species-specific medicinal record.

name: Laver
use: Widely dried and eaten as food by many Pacific coast peoples
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no confident medicinal record.

name: Kombu-like Kelp
use: Eaten and used to wrap food for cooking
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no species-specific medicinal record beyond generic kelp facts.

name: Eelgrass
people: Cape Cod and Long Island settler communities
use: Limited food use, and a later settler-era industrial use as dried insulation and upholstery stuffing
note: An interesting industrial-history material rather than a medicine — no medicinal record found, but kept visible for its documented household/industrial use.

name: Kelp Iodine Industry
people: American industrial chemists, including a WWI-era California kelp-potash industry
use: Processed industrially for iodine and potash rather than used as a home remedy
note: The real American 'kelp iodine' story is 19th–20th century industrial/commercial chemistry, not a home remedy tied to a specific community — included as related history rather than a folk remedy.

name: Sugar Kelp
use: Eaten as food
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no species-specific medicinal record.

name: Winged Kelp (American Wakame)
use: Eaten as food, prepared like Japanese wakame
note: Food-only as far as the research could confirm — no species-specific medicinal record.

name: Puffball for Sores (Yuki)
use: Puffball fungus used as a healing agent for sores; the same kind of puffball was also used as a rattle by a medicine man
note: Journal of Ethnobiology review citing Chestnut's early California ethnobotany. The sores use has no real preparation detail, and the rattle use is ceremonial/material rather than medicinal, so both stay unconfirmed and thin.

name: Puffball Necklace for Respiratory Protection (Blackfoot)
use: Dried puffballs strung into necklaces or bandoliers and worn as a protective charm believed to ward off respiratory disease
note: A protective belief/amulet practice rather than something taken or applied. Included as documented material culture — there is no established protective effect, so it should not be read as prevention advice.

name: Puffball Spore Powder for Burns (Secwepemc)
use: Stored, dried puffball spore powder spread repeatedly over a severe burn, recalled in one family's oral history as home care used after hospital treatment
note: A single family oral-history account rather than a broadly documented practice — thin, one-off detail. Applying stored, nonsterile spore powder to burned skin is not something to try.

name: Puffball Wound Care (Inuit, Nunavik)
use: Puffball spores applied directly to wounds to speed healing, and puffball material shaped into bandages
note: Documented as ordinary wound-care material among northern Inuit communities. Modern sterile wound care is clearly preferable, but this is a genuine, separately documented northern practice worth keeping visible.

name: Serviceberry Eye & Ear Drops (Blackfoot)
use: Berry juice, or a decoction of dried berries, used as eardrops for ear trouble, and dripped into the eye (then covered with a piece of soft hide) for eye trouble
note: The archive's confirmed Saskatoon Serviceberry entry covers digestive, laxative, cough/cold, and children's-appetite uses for Blackfoot, Cheyenne & Cree — it doesn't mention eye or ear application, which is what this record specifically documents.

name: Serviceberry in Ceremony & Belief (Blackfoot & Cheyenne)
use: A blessed ceremonial berry soup served at events such as the opening of a Medicine Pipe or Beaver bundle (Blackfoot); a nursing mother drinking a serviceberry-and-chokecherry infusion in the belief its medicine would pass to her baby (Blackfoot); and smashed fruit added as an ingredient into other, unspecified medicinal mixtures (Cheyenne)
note: These are ceremonial and belief-based uses rather than remedies for a specific symptom, and the 'ingredient in medicinal mixtures' detail is especially thin since the mixture itself isn't recorded. Kept as documented cultural practice, not treatment instruction.

name: Serviceberry Root Tea (Woodlands Cree)
use: Root decoction taken for teething sickness in children, and separately for chest pains and lung infections
note: A root-based tradition from a different nation than the berry-based Blackfoot/Cheyenne uses already in the archive's confirmed Saskatoon Serviceberry entry, which doesn't mention root preparations or Woodlands Cree specifically.

name: American Beautyberry Root for Stomachache (Koasati)
use: Root decoction taken for stomachache
note: The archive's confirmed American Beautyberry Root Sweat Bath entry already covers Alabama, Choctaw & Koasati use for rheumatism, fever, colic, and dysentery — plain stomachache is a distinct symptom not listed there. Detail beyond 'root decoction taken' is thin.

name: Hickory Nuts as Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Caddo region and East Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Hickory nuts, including black hickory (Carya texana), eaten raw, boiled and leached, parched and stored, ground into meal, or pounded for oil added to stews
note: A food/subsistence practice rather than a medicine, drawn from Texas archaeological synthesis rather than a named nation. Included as genuine food-heritage history rather than dropped for being 'just food.'

name: Flowering Dogwood Bark for Sores & as a Blood Purifier (Cherokee & Rappahannock)
use: Bark poultice applied to sores and ulcers (Cherokee); root bark taken internally for diarrhea, as a tonic, and for 'blood purification' (Rappahannock)
note: The archive's confirmed Flowering Dogwood Root & Bark Medicine entry already covers headache, fever, body aches, and general tonic use for these nations — sores/ulcers and diarrhea/blood-purification are additional documented uses not listed there.

name: Persimmon-Wood Massage Stamper (Cherokee)
use: A stamper carved from persimmon wood used to massage patients for rheumatic pain — the wood itself as a physical therapeutic tool, not a preparation taken or applied to the body
note: Distinct in kind from the archive's confirmed American Persimmon Bark entry (sore throat, toothache, hemorrhoids, thrush, bowel complaints, heartburn from the bark) — this is a wooden massage tool, a different sort of remedy entirely.

name: Dried Persimmon Cakes (Cherokee)
use: Ripe fruit seeded, pounded, flattened into cakes, and sun-dried for winter food storage
note: A food-preservation practice, not a medicine. Kept here as genuine subsistence and heritage knowledge rather than dropped as 'just food.'

name: Tinder Fungus — Additional Traditional Uses
people: North American Indigenous peoples (specific nation not recorded in the source review)
use: Reported traditional use as a diuretic and laxative, to calm the nerves, and for rheumatism — beyond the moxibustion-for-rheumatism practice already documented for the Okanagan-Colville nation
note: The source review doesn't name a nation or preparation for these additional uses, so this is a thin, low-confidence lead distinct from the archive's already-confirmed Okanagan-Colville rheumatism/moxibustion entry for the same fungus.

name: White Ash Cambium as Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Inner cambium layer cooked and eaten
note: A food-survival use from Texas archaeological synthesis, not tied to a named nation and not a medicine — kept as genuine subsistence history.

name: Yaupon Holly Black/White Drink Ceremony (Apalachee, Creek, Muskogee & Seminole)
use: Dried, roasted leaves brewed into a dark, caffeinated 'black drink' used for ceremonial purification before ball games and trials (Apalachee), and in the broader Southeastern 'white/black drink' purification ceremony (Creek, Muskogee & Seminole)
note: The archive's confirmed Yaupon Holly Tea entry credits this only vaguely to 'Southeastern Indigenous nations' for general ceremonial/wellness use — this record names the specific nations and the historical black-drink ceremony. It was a sacred, closed practice, not a casual recipe to imitate.

name: Black Walnut Leaf Remedies (Comanche & Delaware)
use: Leaves pulverized and applied for ringworm (Comanche); leaves used as a household flea repellent (Delaware)
note: The archive's confirmed Black Walnut Bark Medicine entry covers Cherokee & Delaware bark use as a cathartic, emetic, and toothache remedy — these are leaf-based uses for a different nation pairing and different purposes (a skin treatment and a pest-control practice, not internal medicine).

name: Black Walnut Nuts as Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Nuts eaten raw, and boiled to render oil
note: A food use, not a medicine, from Texas archaeological synthesis without a named nation — kept as real food heritage distinct from the bark-medicine entry already in the archive.

name: Sweetgum Resin Salve for Skin Complaints (Cherokee)
use: Rosin mixed with sheep or cow tallow and applied topically for itches, cuts, sores, wounds, and cankers; plant material used as a poultice ('drawing plaster') for bruises and sores
note: The archive's confirmed Sweetgum Resin Salve & Tea entry already covers diarrhea, dysentery, anxiety, and 'skin wounds' broadly — this adds the specific rosin-and-tallow salve recipe and named ailments (itches, cankers, bruises) not spelled out there.

name: Red Mulberry Bark for Worms (Cherokee)
use: Bark preparation ingested historically to expel intestinal worms
note: The archive's confirmed Red Mulberry Root & Bark entry covers urinary complaints, ringworm, and constipation for these nations — intestinal worms is a distinct symptom not listed there. No prep detail beyond 'bark preparation ingested' survives in the source.

name: East Texas Pineywoods Forest Resources
people: Indigenous and settler communities of the East Texas Pineywoods (regional/ecological record, not nation-specific)
use: A catalog of the region's medicinally, materially, and edibly significant trees: sweetgum, sassafras, dogwood, black gum, yaupon, beautyberry, black cherry, oaks, hickories, elm, and holly, alongside the native longleaf, shortleaf, and loblolly pines that structure the forest
note: This is a landscape/context summary from the source spreadsheet, not a specific remedy — it names the forest's useful species rather than describing a particular practice. Kept for completeness rather than dropped as too general.

name: White Pine Resin for Wounds & Infection (Cherokee & Ojibwe)
use: Resin used topically on wounds and inflammation (Cherokee), and on infected tissue including gangrene (Ojibwe)
note: The archive's confirmed White Pine Needle Tea entry covers coughs, congestion, and respiratory complaints from Haudenosaunee and other Northeastern nations — this is a resin-based topical wound use for different nations, not a tea.

name: Black Cherry Bark Medicine (Cherokee, Delaware, Iroquois & Lumbee)
use: Bark medicine used, with some variation by community, for cough, colds and flu, fever, worms, and diarrhea
note: Distinct from the archive's confirmed Wild Cherry Bark Syrup entry, which is specifically an Appalachian settler syrup for spasmodic cough — this documents Indigenous-nation bark use across a broader symptom list. Exact preparation wasn't recovered from the primary sources cited.

name: Chokecherry Bark for Pregnancy & Sore Throat (Great Plains Indigenous nations)
people: Great Plains Indigenous nations (multiple, not individually specified in the source)
use: Inner bark tea taken historically as a pregnancy tonic, and used as a gargle for sore throat
note: The archive's confirmed Chokecherry entry already covers digestive and respiratory complaints for these same Plains nations — pregnancy tonic and sore throat are additional documented uses not listed there.

name: Oak Leaves for Ceremonial Cleansing (Ramah Navajo)
use: Leaves used as an emetic for ceremonial cleansing, rather than as an everyday tonic
note: Distinct from the archive's already-unconfirmed oak entries for eye problems (Santa Ysabel Diegueño & Kawaiisu) and cough (Miwok) — this is a different nation, plant part, and a ceremonial rather than symptom-treating use.

name: Acorns as Staple Food (Multiple Indigenous Groups)
people: Multiple Indigenous groups across Texas and North America (not nation-specific in the source)
use: Acorns shelled, ground, leached and rinsed to remove tannins, then cooked as meal, mush, or bread
note: A food-staple practice, not a medicine — processing knowledge that turned an astringent nut into a staple crop. Kept as real food heritage alongside the archive's other oak entries.

name: Red Oak in Cherokee Material Culture & Food (Cherokee)
use: Wood used to keep a sacred eternal fire burning; inner bark fashioned into baskets; acorns sometimes used to make kenuche (a traditional hickory-nut dish)
note: The archive's already-unconfirmed Red Oak for Heart Problems entry (Cherokee) is a medicinal use — these are three separate non-medicinal, material-culture and food uses of the same tree, kept together since they share the nation and species.

name: Smooth Sumac Berries for Vomiting (Cherokee)
use: Red berries eaten historically as an antiemetic, to induce vomiting
note: A direct fruit-based use distinct from the archive's confirmed Sumac Berry Syrup entry (Cherokee, for diarrhea and digestive upset) — vomiting is a different, more deliberate effect than settling digestive upset.

name: Smooth Sumac Root & Flower Remedies (Chippewa/Ojibwe)
use: A decoction of an abnormal growth or gall on the plant used for dysentery; root infusion taken for colds and separately used as an emetic; a compound flower decoction used as a mouthwash for a teething child
note: Distinct nation, plant parts, and uses from the archive's confirmed Smooth Sumac Wash entry (sore throat, mouth complaints, diarrhea, skin conditions for 'Plains & Eastern Indigenous nations' generally) — dysentery, colds, deliberate emesis, and a pediatric compound mouthwash aren't covered there.

name: Smooth Sumac Root Uses (Meskwaki)
use: Root decoction taken as an appetite stimulant for invalids, and root bark used deliberately to raise a blister on the skin as a counterirritant treatment
note: The appetite-stimulant use is thin but plausible household medicine. The blister-raising practice is a genuinely different matter — see caution.
caution: Deliberately raising a blister on the skin with root bark as a counterirritant is a real historical folk practice, but it can cause burns, scarring, and infection. This is documented history, not a technique to try.

name: Smooth Sumac for Earache (Micmac)
use: Plant parts used for earache; the exact part and preparation were not recorded in the surviving source
note: A named-nation, named-ailment record with almost no preparation detail — kept visible as a lead rather than dropped, but genuinely too thin to act on.

name: Black Willow Root Bark for Fever (Cherokee, Houma & Koasati)
use: Bitter root and bark decoction taken as a depurative and for intermittent and other fevers
note: The archive's confirmed Willow Bark Tea entry is deliberately unspecified as to willow species and credited only to 'Woodland Indigenous nations & European settlers alike' — this is a distinct, more specific attribution to Black Willow and three named Southern nations, worth keeping separate rather than folded in.

name: Sassafras Root for Diarrhea & as a Blood Builder (Cherokee)
use: Root tea brewed and taken for diarrhea, and root consumed as what old records call a 'blood builder'
note: The archive's confirmed Cherokee Sassafras Medicine entry covers spider bites, scrofula, sprains, bruises, and sore or infected eyes — diarrhea and the 'blood builder' tonic use are additional Cherokee sassafras uses not listed there.

name: Sphagnum Moss for Hygiene & Utility (Potawatomi & Ojibwe)
use: Moss used as an absorbent material for menstrual cycles and baby diapers (Potawatomi), and gathered and dried as general absorbent and mattress material (Ojibwe)
note: The archive's confirmed Sphagnum Moss Dressing entry covers wound dressing and absorbent lining for wounds — these are separate hygiene and household-utility uses, not wound care, worth keeping distinct.

name: Northern White Cedar Steam & Tea (Mi'kmaq, Menominee, Ojibwe & Iroquois)
use: Leaves or inner bark taken as an infusion for cough (Mi'kmaq); leaves steamed and the vapor inhaled in a sweat-lodge context for colds, headache, fever, and rheumatism (Menominee, Ojibwe & Iroquois-related records)
note: The archive's confirmed Northern White Cedar Tea entry already covers fever, colds, and respiratory complaints for Ojibwe and 'other Great Lakes' nations — this adds Mi'kmaq specifically (not a Great Lakes nation) and a distinct steam-inhalation method for headache and rheumatism.

name: Elm Inner Bark as Emergency Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Inner bark pulverized and cooked into cakes as emergency food
note: A survival-food practice, not a medicine, without a named nation in the source — kept as genuine subsistence history.

name: Lowbush Blueberry in Ceremony (Iroquois)
use: Recorded in an indexed ethnobotanical source as having a ceremonial medicinal role, distinct from everyday food use
note: The archive's confirmed Lowbush Blueberry Medicine entry already covers gastrointestinal complaints, gynecological complaints, and blood medicine for Algonquin (Quebec), Ojibwe & Iroquois — ceremonial use is a distinct category not listed there. The exact ceremony and preparation were not recoverable from the indexed summary, so this is genuinely thin.

name: Smooth Beardtongue
use: Leaves used for snakebite and muscle cramps
note: Reported as a Plains remedy, but no specific nation or preparation method is named, and the source itself notes there is no real evidence it worked as a snakebite antidote.

name: Old World Licorice
use: Listed among "bitter roots and barks" in African American rootwork tradition
note: Appears only as a bare name in a rootwork list, with no preparation method or specific detail beyond the mention; distinct from the archive's confirmed native Wild Licorice Root, a different species.

name: Kola Nut
use: Named as a stimulant root in rootwork tradition
note: Appears only as a bare name in a rootwork list of stimulant roots, with no preparation method or further detail given.

name: Gum-Tree Leaves
people: Gullah/Geechee communities of the Southeast coast
use: Documented as part of Gullah/Geechee ethnobotanical medicinal-plant knowledge
note: Named in a Gullah/Geechee plant list with no stated ailment or preparation method given.

name: John the Conqueror Root (High John Root)
use: Culturally significant root in African American rootwork/hoodoo tradition
note: Well known culturally, but this source gives no specific medicinal ailment or preparation method, so nothing more specific could be written without inventing it.

name: Black Snakeroot
use: Named in a Gullah/Geechee ethnobotanical plant list as a general medicinal root
note: Ambiguous which plant this name refers to (it may overlap with the archive's confirmed Black Cohosh or be a separate species), and no specific use or method is given either way.

name: Late Boneset
use: General traditional medicinal use
note: Included in a plant-chemistry screening study; only a generic "traditional medicinal use" is asserted, with no specific people or preparation method given. A distinct species from the archive's confirmed Boneset Tea.

name: Oak Bark
people: Historical North American medicine generally; specific community unstated
use: Astringent remedy for diarrhea, mouth sores, and bleeding
note: The astringent use is real and historically documented, but attributed only to "historical North American medicine" broadly, with no specific people/nation or preparation method given.

name: Thyme
people: European immigrant households generally (no specific community named)
use: Household remedy for chesty cough and congestion
note: Appears repeatedly in modern evidence-review sources as a folk cough remedy, but no source names a specific community, era, or preparation method, and it overlaps with several already-archived herb-tea entries.

name: Coltsfoot
people: European immigrant households (unspecified); distinct from Alaska Native use of a related species
use: Traditional respiratory and cough remedy
note: No specific people, community, or historical preparation method is given in the sources, which also grade it poorly for liver-injury risk; kept distinct from the archive's confirmed Western Coltsfoot Leaf, a different species with documented Alaska Native use.

name: Butterbur
people: European "plague flower" herbal tradition, carried by immigrant households (no specific community confirmed)
use: Traditional headache and cough remedy
note: A real European folk-medicine plant, but no source confirms genuine American settler adoption (distinct from the archive's confirmed native Petasites frigidus); one source explicitly warns against ever preparing it from a wild plant.

name: Pacific Yew
use: General medicinal and material use
note: Two separate research passes flagged some Northwest Indigenous medicinal/material use, but neither could confirm a specific nation, ailment, or preparation method predating the plant's unrelated 1960s-70s fame as the source of the cancer drug Taxol.

name: Kava
people: Pacific Island peoples generally; no specific U.S. community documented
use: Ceremonial and medicinal use among Pacific Island peoples
note: Hawaii is a plausible U.S. connection, but the source makes no Hawaii-specific historical claim, and gives no preparation method or specific timeframe.

name: Blanketflower
people: Plains Indigenous peoples generally (not confidently tied to a specific nation)
use: Skin-ailment remedy
note: Skin-ailment use is documented for Plains peoples generally, but not confidently specific to the Northern Cheyenne, as sometimes claimed.

name: Wild Tomatillo
use: Stomach ailment and wound remedy
note: Some Plains stomach/wound use is recorded, but it is too thin and generic to write up with confidence.

name: Chaga
people: Circumpolar folk-medicine tradition (Russian/Siberian/Finnish); unclear if adopted by any specific U.S. or Canadian Indigenous community
use: General folk-medicine fungus, unspecified ailments
note: A real circumpolar folk-medicine fungus, but predominantly a Russian/Siberian/Finnish tradition; no confident U.S./Canadian Indigenous community-and-method detail could be identified.

name: Partridge Pea
use: General medicinal use recalled among Cherokee tradition; specific ailment unspecified
note: Only a vague, low-confidence recollection of Cherokee use survives in the research notes, with no specific ailment or method that could be confirmed.

name: Lovage (Nondo)
use: Cold remedy, similar to Osha root
note: A real Appalachian osha-like cold remedy, but there is a real risk of conflating its details with the archive's already-confirmed Osha Root, a different but related species, so it was not committed as a distinct fact.

name: Snowberry / Coralberry
use: Eyewash, soap, and skin wash

name: Wild Tarragon

name: Catclaw Acacia

name: Lousewort

note: A vague recollection of muscle-relaxant use in some western tradition, not specific enough to name a nation or method.

name: American Sycamore

note: A vague recollection of bark used for cough/dysentery by some Eastern nations, not specific enough to name a nation or method.

name: Redbud
use: Bark used for diarrhea and pain
note: A moderate recollection of California-tribe bark use for diarrhea and pain, not confident enough to commit as fact rather than a plausible-sounding guess.

name: Thimbleberry
use: Leaf poultice for burns
note: A moderate recollection of a leaf poultice for burns among Pacific NW peoples, not confident enough to commit to as a clean, specific fact.

name: Virgin's Bower
use: Nerve and blood medicine
note: Only generic and uncertain "nerve/blood medicine" mentions are recalled, with no specific method the researcher trusted enough to commit to.

name: Smartweed
use: Rubbed on skin for pain
note: Generic "rubbed on skin for pain" type mentions recur across many smartweed species, but nothing specific to this one could be confirmed.

name: Knotweed
people: European immigrant households (likely inherited Old World lore)
use: Astringent herb remedy
note: Likely inherited Old World astringent-herb lore, but no source can confirm a specific American usage story versus generic transplanted knowledge.

name: Gentian / Bottle Gentian
use: Bitter digestive tonic
note: Recalled only as a generic "bitter digestive tonic," too undifferentiated by people or method to write up confidently.

name: Frogfruit
people: Possibly Latin American/Caribbean-influenced tradition; U.S.-specific community unconfirmed
use: Traditional medicinal use (unspecified ailment)
note: The traditional use the researcher recalls is more Latin American/Caribbean than confirmed as a specifically U.S. historical practice, though the plant itself is native to the southern U.S.

name: American Germander
use: Diuretic; treatment for sores
note: Only generic "diuretic/sores" mentions are recalled, not specific enough to a people or preparation method.

name: Foxglove Beardtongue
people: Unspecified; some Penstemon species have documented tribal uses
use: Toothache and burn remedy
note: Some Penstemon species have documented toothache/burn uses, but the researcher could not confidently pin specifics to this Eastern species or name a tribe.

name: Violet
use: Cough syrup and poultice
note: A plausible settler cough-syrup/poultice use is recalled, but it is too generic/uncertain to commit to as a confident, specific entry.

name: Evening Primrose
people: Indigenous ethnobotanical record and settler households (unspecified nation)
use: Poultice for bruises and skin complaints
note: Recalled from general ethnobotanical knowledge as a poultice plant, but no specific nation, era, or exact method could be confirmed; a modern "oil" extraction product does not match this historical whole-plant use.

name: Pearly Everlasting
use: Poultice for bruises; possibly used in smoking mixtures
note: The bruise-poultice use is recalled generically; the smoking-mixture detail specifically is flagged by the researcher as unreliable memory.

name: Ironweed
use: Bitter tonic; remedy for "female complaints"
note: Only a vague "bitter tonic/female complaints" recollection survives, not specific enough to a people or method.

name: Fleabane / Horseweed
use: Dried and burned as an insect-repellent smudge, or used as snuff for head colds
note: A plausible use pattern, but the researcher flagged it as possibly reflecting pattern-matching from the plant's "flea-repelling" name rather than confirmed documentation.

name: Ragweed

note: Only thin, generic "rubbed on skin for stings" type recall survives, not specific to a people or method.

name: Cinquefoil
use: Chewed for sore throat
note: Only a generic "chewed for sore throat" type recollection survives, not specific enough to a people or method.

name: Agrimony
people: European immigrant households (likely inherited Old World lore)
use: Wound-herb remedy ("sticklewort")
note: Likely inherited Old World wound-herb lore, but no confirmed American-specific usage story exists beyond that general transplanted knowledge.

name: Foamflower
use: Remedy for mouth sores; diuretic
note: A vague "mouth sores/diuretic" recollection survives, too generic to commit to with a specific people or method.

name: Alumroot
people: Unspecified Indigenous tradition (name implies astringent use)
use: Astringent and styptic (bleeding-stopping) remedy
note: A plausible astringent/styptic use is implied by the plant's own name, but specific tribal attribution and method are not solid enough to present as confident fact.

name: Bittercress (Toothwort)
use: Toothache remedy
note: The toothache association implied by the common name may just be doctrine-of-signatures folk etymology rather than documented practice; the researcher could not confirm it reflects actual historical use.

name: Beaver Castoreum

note: A real 19th-century pharmacopeial ingredient, but only confirmed in formal-apothecary use, not tied to a specific folk community or preparation method.

name: Eggshell & Oyster Shell Powder
use: Calcium-source folk remedy
note: A plausible generic calcium-source folk use, but no specific documented method or community could be confirmed.

name: Animal Hide Poultice

note: A real frontier/Plains-era practice recalled by the researcher, but without confidence in a specific people or community attribution.

name: Summer Savory
use: Bee-sting remedy
note: A plausible Pennsylvania German bee-sting use is recalled, but not confident enough to elevate above general Old World herbal lore.

name: Parsley
people: Unspecified American folk tradition (general Western herbalism)
use: Diuretic; remedy for menstrual complaints
note: A plausible diuretic/menstrual folk use exists in general Western herbalism, but no specific American community or method could be confirmed.

name: Daikon Radish
use: Daikon-and-honey cough remedy
note: Plausible if Japanese-American households carried over this remedy, but the researcher is not confident this specific transmission (versus a Japan-only practice) is actually documented.

name: Rice Water
use: Diarrhea remedy
note: A plausible Gullah/Lowcountry rice-water-for-diarrhea remedy, but no confident specific historical source could be found for the link.

name: Tea

note: Some astringent/diarrhea and eyewash folk use is plausible for ordinary black tea, but nothing specific enough beyond generic beverage use could be confirmed.

name: Nutmeg
use: Digestive and sedative remedy
note: A real digestive/sedative folk reputation exists, but no specific American community or method is solid enough, and the one truly specific historical use (a dangerous-dose abortifacient) was too risky/uncertain to responsibly feature.

name: Borax

note: A real historical practice, but only moderate confidence on precise sourcing, and it is ethically sensitive as a genuinely toxic practice for infants.

name: Alum
use: Astringent gargle and styptic
note: A real astringent/gargle/styptic use existed broadly, but lacks a specific-enough community or method beyond generic pharmacy knowledge.

name: Chalk

note: A standard antidiarrheal preparation, but closer to official apothecary practice than a documented specific-community folk story.

name: Iron Rust

note: The "rusty nail" iron-tonic water appears in general American folklore for anemia/weakness, but only with moderate confidence on precise community or detail.

name: Deer Antler
people: Chinese-American herb shops (e.g. Kam Wah Chung-type stores)
use: Tonic material
note: Plausibly stocked by Chinese-American herb shops as an East Asian tonic material, but not confident enough in a specific documented instance.

name: Whey
use: Fever remedy (whey/posset drinks)
note: Whey/posset drinks for fever existed generically in colonial practice, but are not distinct enough on their own to write with confidence.

name: Coconut Oil
use: Skin, hair, and wound care
note: Plausibly a real Native Hawaiian traditional use, but not confident enough in specific tribal/method detail to commit without risking invention.

name: Garlic Necklace (Anti-Worm)
use: Worn by infants to prevent or treat worms
note: Considered but rejected by the researcher as too weakly sourced to present with confidence, even in voice.

name: Saltwater Joint Soak
use: Soak for sore joints
note: Plausible given the occupational context of Azorean whaling/fishing families, but the researcher could not point to it with real confidence.

name: Four Thieves Vinegar
people: French-Canadian tradition (unconfirmed survival into New England)
use: Multi-herb protective/antiseptic vinegar tonic
note: Solid as general old French folklore, but the researcher could not vouch for it having specifically survived into the New England Franco-American immigrant context.

name: Poppy-Seed Sleeping Syrup
use: Sedative syrup for fussy infants
note: Documented in some Germanic/Central European traditions, but the researcher could not confidently place it in Czech/Slovak-American practice specifically, and it sits close to genuinely risky opiate territory.

name: Krupnikas
use: Honey-spice liqueur taken as a cold remedy
note: The drink is real, but the researcher was not confident enough in its specifically medicinal (rather than festive) use to include it as a full entry.

name: Linden Flower Tea (Kwiat Lipy)
people: Polish immigrant households in Chicago's Polish Downtown and other Great Lakes industrial cities
use: Feverish colds and flu, taken hot to bring on a sweat
method: Linden blossoms gathered and dried in early summer were steeped into a strong tea and served hot, often with honey, at the first sign of a cold or fever — the idea being to sweat the illness out before it could settle in.
note: Linden trees (lipa) held a near-sacred place in Polish village life, planted by churches and in town squares and honored at old shrines to “Matka Boska Lipowa,” Our Lady of the Linden. City boulevard trees in Chicago and Detroit let transplanted families keep gathering the same blossoms an ocean away from the village linden they'd grown up under.

name: Raspberry Syrup for Fever (Sok Malinowy)
people: Polish immigrant households across the Pennsylvania coal towns and Great Lakes cities
use: Fever and colds, given hot to break a fever and soothe a sore throat
method: Raspberries were put up each summer as a thick sugared syrup or preserve; a spoonful stirred into a glass of hot water became the first thing reached for when a child spiked a fever or came down with a cold, given as often as needed through the day.
note: Nearly every Polish-American pantry kept a jar of this syrup set aside specifically for sickness rather than eating — a small, deliberate act of stocking a home pharmacy a year in advance, built from whatever fruit the family's own garden or the corner market had given them that summer.

name: Black Radish and Honey (Czarna Rzodkiew z Miodem)
people: Polish immigrant households in the Pennsylvania anthracite coal region
use: Persistent cough
method: A large black radish was hollowed out, packed with honey, and left to stand overnight — sometimes after a light baking — until the radish drew its own bitter juice up into the honey and formed a dark syrup, taken by the spoonful for cough.
note: Black radish kept in the root cellar all winter, unlike delicate summer produce, so this remedy was reliably on hand exactly when the coal-town coughs of January and February were at their worst. Nearly identical versions turn up across Russian and Ukrainian households too, a sign of how old and widely shared the fix really is among Slavic communities generally.

name: Sauerkraut Juice (Sok z Kiszonej Kapusty)
people: Polish immigrant households in Chicago, Milwaukee, and Buffalo's Polish East Side
use: Digestive upset, and historically a winter source of vitamin C
method: The brine drained from a crock of home-fermented cabbage was drunk plain, warmed, or with a little sugar for a sour stomach; the cooked version, kapuśniak (sour cabbage soup), was standard food for anyone recovering from illness or too weak to manage much else.
note: Long before anyone in the family could have named vitamin C, Polish households already understood that a winter without fresh greens meant kapusta kiszona stood between them and scorbutic gum disease — practical wisdom that outlived any scientific explanation, kept alive in tenement and boarding-house kitchens the same way it had been back home.

name: Beet Juice for the Blood (Sok z Buraków na Krew)
people: Polish immigrant households in the Pennsylvania coal towns
use: Anemia and general weakness, believed to “build the blood”
method: Raw beets were grated and pressed for their juice, or simply the deep-red water they'd been boiled in was saved, then given by the glass or spoonful to anyone looking pale, worn down, or recovering from a long illness or blood loss.
note: The reasoning behind it was almost entirely visual, a piece of old sympathetic folk logic: a vegetable that bleeds a color exactly like blood must obviously help replenish it. It's the same reasoning still repeated, half in earnest, by Polish grandmothers today, long after anyone remembers where the idea first came from.

name: Vodka Compress for Fever (Okłady z Wódki)
people: Polish immigrant households in industrial cities and coal towns alike
use: Bringing down a high fever, especially in a feverish child
method: A cloth soaked in cold vodka, sometimes cut with water, was wrung out and laid on the forehead, wrists, or calves — or the limbs were sponged with it directly — using the alcohol's fast evaporation to pull heat from the skin, refreshed again as it warmed.
note: The same bottle kept in the cupboard for holiday toasts did double duty as the sickroom's fever remedy, a piece of pure household thrift that Polish, Russian, and Ukrainian home medicine all arrived at independently, each under its own name.
caution: Alcohol evaporates and cools the skin quickly, but it also absorbs through it — overly generous sponging or compresses have caused real cases of alcohol poisoning in infants and small children, which is why this practice is medically discouraged today.

name: Calendula Ointment (Maść Nagietkowa)
people: Polish immigrant households, from Pittsburgh's Polish Hill to coal-town garden plots
use: Cuts, scrapes, chapped skin, and minor skin infections
method: Calendula petals from the garden were simmered gently into melted lard or oil, then strained and left to cool into a soft ointment kept in a tin for the next scraped knee, cracked hand, or diaper rash.
note: Nagietek was one of the few medicinal plants a family deliberately planted rather than foraged along a roadside — a cheerful, self-seeding flower kept in a corner of the vegetable patch for exactly this purpose — and immigrant households replanted it in city yards and window boxes wherever they landed, from Pittsburgh to the Great Lakes.

name: Plantain Leaf Cough Syrup (Syrop z Babki Lancetowatej)
people: Polish immigrant households in Detroit, Cleveland, and other Great Lakes industrial cities
use: Persistent cough
method: Fresh plantain leaves were layered with sugar or honey in a jar and left to stand for days or weeks until they gave up a dark, thick syrup, which was strained off and given by the spoonful for a cough that wouldn't quit.
note: Babka — literally “little grandmother” — grew wild along every path, fence line, and dooryard, making it one of the few Old World medicinal plants a family could still gather for free from a sidewalk crack or a scrap of city yard, no garden or grocery money required.

name: Blessed Herb Bundle (Matka Boska Zielna)
people: Polish Catholic immigrant households in Chicago and Buffalo's Polish parishes
use: Kept through the year as spiritual protection, and reached for at the first sign of illness
method: On the Feast of the Assumption, August 15th — known in Polish devotion as Matka Boska Zielna, “Our Lady of the Herbs” — a bundle of garden herbs, field flowers, and grain was carried to Mass to be blessed, then dried and kept over a doorway or tucked behind a holy picture; a pinch was later brewed as tea or burned like incense whenever sickness struck the household.
note: The custom folded a purely practical fact inside a religious one: mid-August is exactly when the year's herbs are ready for harvest anyway, so the family's medicine cabinet got restocked and blessed on the same afternoon. Polish parishes in cities like Chicago and Buffalo still hold this same blessing every August 15th.

name: Gromnica (Blessed Candle)
people: Polish Catholic immigrant households in the Pennsylvania coal region
use: Invoked for protection during serious illness, violent storms, and at a deathbed
method: A candle blessed at Mass on February 2nd — Candlemas, called in Polish Matki Bożej Gromnicznej — was wrapped away in a drawer the rest of the year and lit only in crisis: set in the window during a bad thunderstorm, or burned at the bedside of someone dying, to ease the passing and keep harm at a distance.
note: The candle's name comes straight from grom, “thunder,” reflecting its double duty against both storms and sickness. Immigrant families carried the custom of the deathbed gromnica faithfully into their new parish churches, and it's still remembered by older parishioners in Polish-American communities today.

name: Amber Teething Necklace (Naszyjnik z Bursztynu)
people: Polish immigrant households, especially those with family still on the Baltic coast
use: Easing teething pain in infants, and worn for general protection
method: A baby was dressed in a short strand of raw or polished amber beads worn against the skin, believed to ease the discomfort of teething and guard the child against illness generally; pieces were sometimes specially requested from relatives still living back in Poland.
note: Poland's Baltic coast, especially around Gdańsk, has been one of the world's great amber sources since antiquity — the old “Amber Road” trade routes ran straight through it — which gave amber an outsized cultural weight for Polish families that ordinary jewelry never carried.
caution: Amber teething necklaces are now recognized as a real choking and strangulation hazard for infants, and pediatric guidance today advises against them regardless of the old belief in their benefit.

name: Poppy Pod Tea (Herbata z Makówek)
people: Polish immigrant households in Pennsylvania's coal and mill towns
use: Historically, to quiet a restless or colicky baby, and to ease a bad cough
method: Dried poppy seed pods left over from the household's own poppy harvest — grown for the black seed used in holiday baking, not for any narcotic purpose — were boiled into a mild tea given by the spoonful to settle a fussy infant or calm a persistent cough.
note: The same poppy plants that produced the black seed for Christmas kołacz and makowiec pastries also produced these leftover pods, so the “medicine” and the holiday dessert came from the same row in the garden. It was exactly this kind of quiet, well-meant home practice that alarmed public-health reformers investigating immigrant tenement neighborhoods in the early 1900s.
caution: Poppy pods contain real opiate alkaloids, including morphine and codeine. This practice carried a genuine risk of overdose in infants and is not remotely safe by modern standards — it appears here strictly as a documented historical practice, not a recommendation.

name: Flaxseed Mucilage Drink (Kisiel z Siemienia Lnianego)
people: Polish immigrant households in Great Lakes industrial cities
use: Sore throat and cough, and to settle an irritated stomach
method: Whole flaxseed was simmered in water until it released a thick, slippery mucilage, which was strained, sweetened with a little honey, and sipped warm to coat and soothe an irritated throat.
note: Flax was grown across the Polish countryside for its fiber and oil as much as for uses like this one, so the seed was cheap, familiar, and reliably on hand — one Old World ingredient an immigrant family didn't have to hunt down or substitute for in an unfamiliar American grocery.

name: Horsetail Tea for the Kidneys (Herbata ze Skrzypu Polnego)
people: Polish immigrant households in the Pennsylvania coal region
use: Kidney and bladder complaints, water retention, and as a general diuretic tonic
method: Dried horsetail stems were steeped into a tea and drunk for water retention and bladder discomfort, and kept up as an everyday tonic said to strengthen brittle nails and hair through its mineral content.
note: Skrzyp polny remains one of the most common single herbs in Polish kidney-and-bladder tea blends sold in pharmacies to this day — a rare case of an old dooryard weed that walked straight into the modern herbal-medicine aisle without ever really leaving Polish households in between.
caution: Its diuretic effect is real; long-term use, or use by anyone with existing kidney disease, calls for medical guidance rather than home dosing alone.

name: Chá de Macela (Wild Chamomile Tea)
people: Azorean Portuguese-American households, especially in New Bedford and Fall River, Massachusetts
use: Infant colic, gas, and upset stomach
method: Dried macela flowers — a small, mild, apple-scented daisy relative, distinct from German chamomile — were steeped into a very weak tea, sweetened lightly, and given to fussy infants by spoon or bottle; adults drank a stronger cup for the same complaints.
note: Macela was considered gentle enough for newborns and was often the first tea a Portuguese-American mother reached for, grown when possible in a pot on the back steps of a triple-decker mill-town tenement rather than a proper garden.

name: Chá de Tília (Linden Flower Tea)
people: Portuguese and Azorean immigrant households in New England
use: Sleeplessness, nervous tension, and being "nervoso"
method: Dried linden flowers and bracts were steeped in hot water for a few minutes and drunk before bed, often with a little honey; it was considered the mildest household remedy for a racing mind or a fretful child.
note: Tília was one of the few herbs a Portuguese immigrant family was likely to buy dried and bagged from a home-country grocer rather than grow themselves, since linden trees were harder to come by in a Massachusetts mill town than back home — it is still a common household tea today.

name: Chá de Erva-Cidreira (Lemon Balm Tea)
people: Portuguese and Azorean immigrant households in New England
use: Nervous stomach, mild anxiety, and trouble sleeping
method: Fresh or dried lemon balm leaves were steeped into a mild, lemon-scented tea, taken in the evening or whenever someone was feeling "aborrecido" — fretful, out of sorts.
note: Nearly every Azorean-American dooryard or windowsill kept a pot of erva-cidreira going, since a cup of it was the standard first response to almost any complaint that wasn't already something more specific.

name: Panos de Vinagre (Vinegar Compress for Fever)
people: Portuguese and Azorean immigrant households in New England
use: Bringing down a high fever
method: Cloths were soaked in vinegar diluted with cool water, wrung out, and laid across the forehead and the soles of the feet, changed every so often until the fever eased; some families also rubbed diluted vinegar over the wrists and the back of the neck.
note: Treating the feet as carefully as the forehead reflected an old-country belief that a fever needed to be drawn downward and out of the body, not just cooled at the head.

name: Resguardo (Forty Days of Postpartum Care)
people: Azorean Portuguese-American new mothers and their families in New England
use: Postpartum recovery
method: For about forty days after giving birth, a new mother stayed close to home, kept warm, ate mild cooked foods like broths, chicken, and rice instead of anything considered "cold" or hard to digest, and avoided drafts, cold water, and heavy work, while female relatives took over the household and the cooking.
note: The rule was never really about temperature on a thermometer — it came from an old hot/cold way of understanding the body, quente and frio, in which a new mother was seen as dangerously open to "cold" getting into her, whatever the weather actually was outside the tenement window.

name: Quebranto and the Benzedeira's Blessing
people: Azorean Portuguese-American families in New England
use: A fretful, listless baby or child believed to be suffering from quebranto — a fright- or evil-eye-like sickness with no clearer cause
method: An older woman known locally for the gift of "benzer" (blessing) said a set of quiet prayers over the child, often making the sign of the cross over its body or passing her hands near it, sometimes repeating the blessing over three days running.
note: Quebranto was understood as something apart from ordinary illness — closer to being "broken" by too much admiring attention or a bad look than to catching a germ — and a mother might seek out a known benzedeira before she thought to call a doctor.

name: Milagres and the Feast of Senhor Santo Cristo
people: Azorean Portuguese-American Catholics, especially in Fall River, Massachusetts
use: Seeking healing for a specific illness or injury, through prayer and a vowed act of devotion
method: A person seeking healing, or giving thanks for it, made a "promessa" (vow) to Senhor Santo Cristo dos Milagres — praying before the image, sometimes walking the annual procession barefoot, or leaving behind a small wax or metal charm shaped like the afflicted body part once the vow was fulfilled.
note: The devotion crossed the Atlantic in 1897, carried directly from the Convent of Esperança in Ponta Delgada, São Miguel, by Azorean immigrants in Fall River — it grew into the largest Portuguese religious festival in the United States, built quite literally around the idea of miraculous healing, since milagres means miracles.

name: Cravo (Clove) for Toothache
use: Toothache
method: A whole clove was held against the aching tooth and gum, or chewed gently to release its numbing oil, to get a family through until a dentist could be seen — often a good while, when spare cash was scarce.
note: A tin of whole cloves in a kitchen drawer was as much a part of the household medicine chest as any tea, and small and portable enough to travel with a family from the Azores to a New England tenement.

name: Casca de Romã (Pomegranate Rind Tea)
use: Diarrhea and loose bowels
method: The dried inner rind of a pomegranate was boiled into a strongly astringent tea, taken in small doses until symptoms settled.
note: Pomegranate trees were scarce in New England, so the dried rind was one of the old-country remedies a family might set aside from fruit sent up by relatives, or buy already dried at a Portuguese grocer down the street from the mill.

name: Marmelada (Quince Paste) for Upset Stomach
use: Diarrhea and a sour, unsettled stomach
method: A spoonful of homemade marmelada — quince cooked down slowly with sugar into a thick, firm paste — was given plain, or the quince itself was simmered into a decoction and sipped, for its natural astringency.
note: The English word "marmalade" actually comes from marmelada, the Portuguese word for this quince paste — the word crossed into English centuries before the citrus preserve did, though few New England neighbors spreading orange marmalade on toast would have known that.

name: Graisse de Siffleux (Groundhog Fat) Chest Rub
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) mill-town families of New England
use: Bronchitis, chest colds, and croup
method: Fat rendered from a groundhog was warmed until liquid, rubbed onto the chest and back, and covered with a piece of wool flannel overnight; the smell alone was said to be enough to loosen a child's cough.
note: Graisse de siffleux is one of the most fondly — and most sheepishly — remembered remedies of Quebecois and Franco-American childhood, the kind of thing grown children still bring up at family gatherings half in disgust and half in real affection for a grandmother's care.

name: Sirop d'Érable (Maple Syrup) for Cough
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) households of New England and the Great Lakes region
use: Cough and sore throat
method: Maple syrup was taken warm by the spoonful, sometimes stirred into hot water or milk with a little butter, to coat and soothe a raw throat; in early spring, some families also drank the raw sap straight from the tap, on the belief that a cup of it fresh from the tree helped clear out the winter.
note: Maple sugaring was one of the few pieces of rural Quebec life a mill-town family could keep up even from a city tenement, since relatives back on the farm would send syrup and sugar along whenever someone traveled between Quebec and a New England "Petit Canada" neighborhood.

name: Racine de Bardane (Burdock Root) Spring Tonic
use: Spring "blood purifying" tonic, and skin complaints like acne and eczema
method: The root was dug in fall or early spring, sliced, and boiled down into a bitter decoction taken by the cupful for a few weeks each spring, or simmered longer into a stronger wash applied directly to troublesome skin.
note: Like the nettle and dandelion tonics of other traditions, bardane tied a household's health to the turning of the seasons — a low, tired late-winter feeling was something to be treated with a root dug from the ground, not with anything bought at a shop.

name: Le Rebouteux (The Bonesetter)
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) mill-town and Great Lakes farming communities
use: Broken bones, dislocations, sprains, and pulled muscles
method: A rebouteux — a self-taught bonesetter with a local reputation for a healer's hands, more often than not a farmer or laborer with no formal training at all — manipulated, pulled, and splinted an injury on the kitchen table, long before a family would spend money on a doctor for anything short of a true emergency.
note: The rebouteux was a recognized, respected role in rural Quebec long before emigration, and French-Canadian families who settled in Great Lakes farming communities or New England mill towns kept an eye out for one of their own the same way they'd have looked for a good midwife, or a priest who could hear confession in French.

name: Relevailles (Postpartum Rest and Churching)
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) Catholic households of New England
use: Postpartum recovery
method: A new mother kept to her bed and then to the house for roughly a month after giving birth, cared for by female relatives, before a special blessing at the parish church — the relevailles — marked her formal return to Mass and to public life.
note: Large families were both a practical reality of farm and mill-town life and, in the Catholic culture of the era, something close to a civic duty — church and community leaders openly encouraged high birth rates as a way for French-Canadians to hold their ground demographically, a policy still remembered by its old nickname, "la revanche des berceaux," the revenge of the cradle.

name: Pèlerinage à Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré (Healing Pilgrimage)
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) Catholic communities of New England
use: Seeking healing for chronic illness, injury, or disability through prayer and pilgrimage
method: A sick or injured person, or their family on their behalf, traveled — often by parish-organized excursion train — to the shrine of Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré on the St. Lawrence River, to pray for a cure and, if one seemed to come, to leave a crutch, brace, or cane behind at the shrine as proof.
note: For mill-town Franco-American parishes, a trip back to Quebec for Sainte-Anne's feast day in late July was as much a health pilgrimage as a homecoming — families who had left the farm for the mills still went back to ask the same saint their grandparents had, for the same kind of help.

name: Frère André's Blessed Oil
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) Catholic communities, especially in the early 20th century
use: Chronic pain, paralysis, and illnesses that had not responded to ordinary medicine
method: Oil taken from the lamp burning before a statue of Saint Joseph was rubbed onto the afflicted part of the body, following the practice made famous by Brother André Bessette, a lay brother at Montreal's Oratory of Saint Joseph known across French Canada and the diaspora for his healing touch.
note: Brother André's fame reached well past Quebec's borders during his own lifetime — Franco-American families in New England, tied to Montreal by train, family, and faith alike, wrote to him, brought afflicted relatives to see him, or simply kept his picture and a small vial of blessed oil in the house.

name: Sirop de Navet (Turnip Syrup) for Cough
use: Cough and chest colds
method: A turnip was sliced thin, layered with brown sugar or honey in a bowl, and left overnight; the syrup that collected at the bottom was given by the spoonful for cough, the same way other families made a similar syrup from sliced onion or black radish.
note: Almost every French-Canadian household seemed to favor its own particular vegetable for this trick — the remedy was less about the specific plant than about a very old, widely shared kitchen habit of drawing a curative syrup out of a raw vegetable with nothing but sugar and a night's patience.

name: Frotter avec de la Neige (Rubbing Frostbite with Snow)
people: French-Canadian (Franco-American) loggers and farm families of Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota
use: Frostbitten fingers, toes, ears, and noses
method: A frostbitten area was rubbed briskly with snow or packed in it, on the belief that the cold needed to be drawn back out of the skin gradually rather than warmed too fast.
note: French-Canadian lumberjacks made up a large share of the logging camps of the Great Lakes and Maine woods, and some folklorists trace part of the later, heavily Americanized Paul Bunyan legend to French-Canadian camp storytelling carried into those same woods.
caution: This is now known to be the wrong response to frostbite — rubbing or packing frozen tissue in snow worsens the tissue damage. It's included here for historical interest only; modern guidance calls for gentle rewarming in lukewarm water.

name: Linden Flower Tea (Lipový Čaj)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant households in America
use: Colds, fevers, and a mild bedtime calmative for sleeplessness
method: Dried linden (basswood) flowers were steeped as a hot tea, often taken at the first sign of a cold and followed by a warm bed and blankets to “sweat out” the fever; a milder cup was given before bed to settle a restless household.
note: The linden tree (lípa) is practically a Czech national emblem, planted along boulevards and in town squares back home, and often replanted by homesick immigrants near parish halls and Sokol gymnastic-hall lawns in Chicago's Pilsen and Cleveland's old Czech neighborhoods, where the flowers could still be gathered every June.

name: Caraway Seed Soup (Kmínová Polévka)
people: Czech immigrant farm households of Nebraska & Texas
use: Upset stomach and gas, and a gentle first food for new mothers and convalescents
method: Caraway seeds were simmered in broth or water thickened with a little flour and butter, sometimes finished with a poached egg; the plain, mildly aromatic soup was considered easy on a weak stomach when almost nothing else would sit right.
note: Caraway (kmín) is one of the defining flavors of Czech cooking, worked into rye bread and roast pork alike, so keeping a jar of the seeds on hand for a sick house was as ordinary as keeping salt.

name: Garlic Soup (Česnečka)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant laborers, Chicago's Pilsen and Cleveland's Czech neighborhoods
use: Warding off a cold before it took hold, and a hearty meal for those coming off a factory or packinghouse shift
method: Crushed garlic was simmered in broth or water with a little marjoram and caraway, then poured over cubes of dried bread and topped with grated cheese; a stronger version was made at the very first scratchy throat of a coming cold.
note: A bowl of česnečka at the end of a long shift was as much about getting warm and fed as about medicine, but the garlic was never left out, cold season or not.

name: Carlsbad Mineral Salts (Karlovarská Sůl)
people: Czech immigrant households in America, especially those with ties to the spa towns of Bohemia
use: Constipation, indigestion, and “liver trouble”
method: A spoonful of the mineral salt, sold by American druggists as an import (and later a domestic imitation) of the real Karlovy Vary spring salts, was dissolved in a glass of warm water and drunk before breakfast.
note: Back in Bohemia, “taking the cure” at Karlovy Vary's (Carlsbad's) mineral springs was a genuine institution, drawing the wealthy and the merely constipated from across Europe. Immigrant households who couldn't afford the trip could still buy a tin of the actual dried spring salts, or a convincing substitute, from the corner drugstore, a small taste of the old country's most famous export.

name: Goose Fat Skin Salve (Husí Sádlo)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant farm households of Nebraska, Texas & the rural Midwest
use: Chapped hands, cracked heels, and windburned skin through the winter
method: Fat rendered from the goose was strained and kept in a covered crock in a cool pantry; a small amount was worked into rough or cracked skin as needed all winter long.
note: The fat came from the goose killed for St. Martin's Day (Svatomartinská husa) on November 11th, a feast marking the start of the Central European winter, so the salve in the crock and the first frost on the ground tended to arrive at more or less the same time every year.

name: Cold Curd Cheese Compress (Tvarohový Obklad)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant households, Pittsburgh's steel-mill neighborhoods
use: Bringing down a fever, and easing a sore, swollen breast in nursing mothers
method: Fresh curd cheese (tvaroh) was spread cold, about a finger thick, onto a cloth and laid directly against the forehead or the affected area, replaced with a fresh cold portion as it warmed from the body.
note: The same soft farmer's cheese that filled Sunday dumplings and pastries did double duty as the household's go-to cooling compress, cheap, always on hand, and, unlike a plain wet cloth, slow to warm through.

name: Chamomile Steam & Eyewash (Heřmánek)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant households in America
use: A stuffed-up head and sinuses, and sore, irritated or “sticky” eyes
method: For a stuffy head, a handful of chamomile flowers was steeped in a basin of just-boiled water and the face held over the steam under a towel tent. For sore eyes, a much weaker, well-cooled tea was used to bathe the eyes with a clean soft cloth.
note: Heřmánek is close to a household god in Czech home medicine; there's an old saying that translates roughly as “for that, chamomile is good,” trotted out as the reflexive answer to nearly any minor complaint.

name: Lovage (Libeček)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant farm households of Nebraska & Texas
use: Kidney and bladder complaints, poor digestion, and, by old belief, easing labor
method: The root or leaf was simmered into a tea, or the fresh leaf was added generously to soup; lovage was such a fixture of the everyday potato-soup pot that many households hardly distinguished the seasoning from the medicine.
note: Almost every Czech farmyard kitchen garden kept a lovage plant by the door, grown as much for the stockpot as for the medicine chest; its strong, celery-like smell is still the first thing many Czech-Americans associate with their grandmother's soup.

name: Slivovitz (Plum Brandy)
people: Czech & Slovak immigrant households, especially Slovak steelworker families of Pittsburgh & the Pennsylvania mill towns
use: Warming against a cold, settling a heavy meal, and disinfecting a small cut when nothing else was on hand
method: A small glass was taken straight, sometimes warmed, at the first chill of a cold or after a rich Sunday dinner; for a wound, it was poured directly over the cut in place of proper antiseptic.
note: Homemade plum brandy, distilled from backyard or orchard plums, followed Czech and Slovak families from the old country's fruit-growing regions to America almost as faithfully as the recipes for dumplings did; Prohibition slowed but never fully stopped the household still.
caution: High-proof homemade spirits varied widely in strength and were sometimes distilled in unsafe home equipment; pouring spirits directly into an open wound is not a substitute for real wound care.

name: Beer Soup (Pivní Polévka)
people: Czech immigrant households, Chicago & Cleveland's brewing and industrial neighborhoods
use: Building up strength in a nursing mother or a weak convalescent
method: Beer was warmed gently (never boiled hard, or it turned bitter) and thickened with egg yolk beaten with sugar, sometimes with cubes of bread or a splash of cream stirred in at the end.
note: In a community that had followed Bohemian brewing traditions straight into the Midwest's beer-town breweries, it made a certain sense that beer itself, not just garlic or onion, would end up in the sickroom.
caution: Contains alcohol; historically given in small amounts to nursing mothers and convalescents, a practice not recommended today.

name: Blessed Herb Bundle (Bylinky) for the Feast of the Assumption
people: Czech & Slovak Catholic immigrant households in America
use: General protection and healing kept in reserve for whenever illness struck the household
method: A bundle of garden and field herbs, often including yarrow, chamomile, and whatever else was blooming, was brought to church to be blessed on the Feast of the Assumption, August 15th, then hung to dry in the kitchen. A pinch was steeped into tea, or burned like incense, when someone in the house fell ill over the year that followed.
note: Texas's Czech Catholic parish at Praha still holds its well-known Assumption Day pilgrimage and picnic every August, a reminder of how central that particular feast day was to Czech-American Catholic life, far from Bohemia.

name: Kerosene on a Sugar Cube
people: Slovak immigrant coal-mining families of the Pennsylvania anthracite region
use: Suppressing a persistent cough, including a miner's chronic “coal cough”
method: A few drops of kerosene were placed on a sugar cube or spoonful of sugar and swallowed whole, said to break up a stubborn cough that plain sugar syrup couldn't touch.
note: Remedies this rough-and-ready circulated through many of the same coal patches and company towns that Slovak, Rusyn, and other immigrant miners shared, born out of households where the company doctor was expensive, distant, or distrusted.
caution: Kerosene is toxic if swallowed and can cause serious lung damage if aspirated; this remedy is recorded here strictly as a documented historical practice, not a safe one.

name: Black Radish & Honey (Chorna Redka z Medom)
people: Ukrainian & Carpatho-Rusyn immigrant households in America
use: Persistent cough, especially in children
method: The top of a large black radish was sliced off and a deep well carved into the flesh, then packed with honey and left to sit overnight (or set near warmth); the sweet juice that collected in the well was given by the spoonful for a cough.
note: The same trick was worked with turnips in leaner households when a black radish wasn't to be had; the point was the slow-drawn juice, not the particular vegetable, and grandmothers on both sides of the ocean swore by it.

name: Propolis Tincture
people: Ukrainian immigrant households in America, especially those keeping bees, Cleveland's Tremont neighborhood
use: Sore throat, mouth sores, toothache, and disinfecting small cuts
method: Raw propolis, the dark, resinous “bee glue” bees use to seal their hives, was dissolved in strong alcohol over several weeks, strained, and kept as a standing household tincture; a few drops were added to warm water as a gargle, or dabbed directly onto a wound or aching tooth.
note: Beekeeping came to America with Ukrainian immigrant families as more than a hobby; it was a direct continuation of a rural home-medicine cabinet, since propolis, honey, and beeswax together covered a remarkable share of everyday complaints.

name: Kalyna (Guelder Rose) Berry Tea
use: Cough, sore throat, and colds
method: The bright red berries, picked only after the first frost softened their sharp raw taste, were simmered with a little honey into a tea or thick syrup and taken warm for a cough or sore throat.
note: No plant carries more weight in Ukrainian culture than kalyna: it appears in embroidery, in wedding customs, and in the folk song “Chervona Kalyna” (“The Red Kalyna”), which became an anthem of Ukrainian resilience far beyond its use as a home remedy. Homesick immigrants planted the bush by their doorsteps in Pennsylvania and Ohio whenever they could get a start of it.
caution: Raw, unripe kalyna berries are mildly toxic and were always cooked or frost-softened before use.

name: Vodka-and-Water Fever Rub
people: Ukrainian & Rusyn immigrant households in America
use: Bringing down a high fever, especially in children
method: Vodka was diluted about half-and-half with cool water, and a cloth soaked in the mixture was used to sponge down a feverish person's arms, legs, and back, the evaporating alcohol pulling heat from the skin faster than water alone.
note: This was a common-sense household trick passed down through generations of Slavic mothers long before germ theory explained why it worked, or, in some cases, whether it really did.
caution: Alcohol can be absorbed through the skin, especially in young children, and sponging with alcohol is no longer recommended by modern medicine; it is recorded here only as a documented historical practice.

name: Salo with Garlic
people: Ukrainian immigrant households in America, especially Cleveland's Tremont neighborhood
use: Building strength and warding off colds through the winter
method: Cured, salted pork fatback (salo) was sliced thin and eaten on dark rye bread rubbed with a raw garlic clove, especially at the start of the cold season or after heavy labor.
note: Salo occupies an almost sacred place in Ukrainian food culture, jokes about it are a genre unto themselves, and pairing it with raw garlic turned an everyday snack into a half-serious, half-joking cold-prevention ritual that immigrant families kept up in their new American kitchens.

name: Poppy Seeds Against Illness-Bringing Spirits
people: Ukrainian & Rusyn immigrant households in America
use: Protecting a household from illness believed to be caused by evil spirits or a restless dead
method: A handful of poppy seeds was scattered across a doorway, windowsill, or coffin, on the folk belief that a wandering spirit would be compelled to stop and count every single seed before it could cross, by which time morning, and safety, would arrive.
note: This belief belongs to a much older, widespread Slavic folk tradition about restless spirits and the dead, but it traveled to America inside the same trunks as the herb bundles and the icons, repurposed by worried households as one more layer of protection during a bad flu season or a death in the neighborhood.

name: Blessing of Herbs (Sviachennia Zillia)
people: Ukrainian Greek Catholic & Orthodox immigrant households in America
use: General household protection and healing kept in reserve for the coming year
method: Bundles of field herbs, flowers, and grain, sometimes with poppy heads or dill included, were brought to the Eastern-rite church to be blessed at the August feasts of the Transfiguration and the Dormition of the Mother of God, then dried and kept at home; a pinch was steeped into tea, or the smoke of the burning herbs passed over a sick person, when illness came.
note: Coal-town parishes like Shenandoah, Pennsylvania's, home to one of the earliest Carpatho-Rusyn Greek Catholic congregations in America, founded in the 1880s, carried this blessing across the ocean along with the rest of the Eastern-rite calendar that shaped the immigrant year.

name: Garlic on a String
people: Ukrainian & Rusyn immigrant households in America
use: Warding off colds and flu at school, and, by old belief, warding off the evil eye
method: Whole garlic cloves were strung on a thread and hung around a child's neck under their clothing before they left for school during a bad cold-and-flu season.
note: The same clove that went into the soup pot did guard duty around a child's neck; practical medicine and protective charm were never really separated in these households, just two sides of the same clove.

name: Warmed Buckwheat Groats Ear Pillow
use: Earache
method: Dry buckwheat groats were warmed in a dry pan or the oven, poured into a small cloth bag or the toe of a sock, and held warm against the aching ear until the pain eased.
note: Buckwheat (hrechka) held the same everyday, foundational place in the Ukrainian kitchen that potatoes held in Irish ones, so it was the grain closest to hand to fill a warm pack with, whatever the ailment.

name: Dill Water for Nursing Mothers
people: Ukrainian & Rusyn immigrant households in America
use: Encouraging a nursing mother's milk supply
method: Dill seed, or a handful of the fresh feathery leaf, was steeped into a tea and drunk warm by the nursing mother several times a day.
note: Dill (krip) was grown in nearly every immigrant kitchen garden for the pickle barrel and the borscht pot alike, so it cost a new mother nothing extra to lean on it as a nursing tonic too.

name: Sauerkraut Brine (Rozsil)
use: A sour stomach, poor digestion, and the morning after too much drink
method: The salty, sour liquid left in the barrel or crock after a batch of sauerkraut had fully fermented was drunk by the glassful, plain or slightly warmed.
note: A cellar full of fermenting cabbage was as much a fixture of the immigrant winter pantry as coal in the bin, and its leftover brine as a hangover cure has stayed a half-joking, half-serious point of pride in Ukrainian households ever since.

name: Mustard-Rye Plaster
people: Rusyn & Ukrainian immigrant coal-mining families of the Pennsylvania anthracite region
use: Chest congestion, bronchitis, and a miner's persistent chest cold
method: Dry mustard powder was mixed with rye flour and warm water into a paste (the flour cut down on how badly the mustard could blister the skin), spread on a cloth, and bound to the chest under a warm shirt until the skin turned pink and glowing.
note: In a coal patch where the company doctor might be a mile off and cost a half-day's pay to see, the household babka (grandmother) making up a mustard plaster was often the first and only treatment a bad chest cold ever got.
caution: Left on too long, a mustard plaster can blister the skin; it was checked and removed well before that point.

name: Blessed Water at Theophany (Yordan)
people: Ukrainian Greek Catholic & Orthodox immigrant households in America
use: General healing and protection, drunk or sprinkled when illness struck
method: Water blessed at church on the feast of Theophany (Yordan), commemorating Christ's baptism in the Jordan River, was carried home in jugs and bottles and kept year-round; a sick person might be given a sip of it, or have a little sprinkled over them, alongside whatever other remedy was in use.
note: Immigrant parishes kept the old custom going every January, and a bottle of that year's blessed water sitting on a kitchen shelf, refilled annually, was a fixture of religious and medicinal life at once in these households.

name: Cupping (Banky)
people: Ukrainian, Rusyn & Lithuanian immigrant coal- and steel-town families
use: Chest colds, bronchitis, and back and muscle pain
method: A bit of cotton on a wire or fork was dipped in alcohol, lit, and passed briefly inside a small drinking glass to heat the air, then the glass was pressed quickly to the back or chest; as the trapped air cooled it drew the skin up into the glass, leaving a ring-shaped mark behind.
note: Almost every Eastern European immigrant grandmother seems to be remembered doing some version of banky on a husband's aching back after a shift underground or at the mill, a piece of home medicine common across Slavic and Baltic households alike, mechanically not so different from what Italian, Jewish, and other immigrant neighbors were doing with their own cupping glasses down the same street.

name: Amber (Gintaras) Teething Necklace
people: Lithuanian immigrant communities in America, including the coal town of Shenandoah, Pennsylvania
use: Easing a teething baby's pain and, by old belief, guarding a child's general health
method: A necklace of small polished Baltic amber beads was tied loosely around a teething infant's neck, worn under clothing against the skin, on the folk belief that the body's warmth released the amber's soothing properties.
